This first D&SMA class, with Prof Bindhia Joji, taught you to read data visuals, trace why traffic does not turn into sales, tell KPIs from metrics and analysis from analytics, and build dashboards that tell a story. It ended with a delivery-delay dataset exercise.

## Key terms

| Term | Meaning | Class example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conversion | A visitor taking the desired action, such as buying | Ad click to checkout |
| Conversion rate | Conversions divided by visitors | Offline: buyers divided by walk-ins |
| KPI | A key performance indicator: a measure tied to a goal | Conversion rate |
| Metric | Any number that measures something | Page views |
| Cart abandonment | Shoppers adding items but leaving before paying | A reason traffic does not convert |
| Analysis | Studying past and present data to understand it | Power BI charts |
| Analytics | Using data to predict what comes next | Forecasting sales |
| Dashboard | A visual summary of KPIs that tells a story | About two KPIs per page |
| GA4 | Google Analytics 4, the current web analytics standard | Tracking cost per order and CLV |

## Reading any data visual

1. Understand what the chart shows.
2. Interpret what it means.
3. Decide the action.

**Class example:** Use a line chart for a trend over months or quarters, such as low in Q1 rising to Q4. Use a bar chart when data is uneven across categories.
**Class example:** If page views rise but conversions stay low, open a different visual to find where people drop off.
**Exam tip:** Always end a chart interpretation with an action. "Views rose 40%" is analysis; "move the offer higher on the page" is what earns marks.

## Conversion on Instagram and e-commerce

**Definition:** Conversion is when a visitor takes the action you want, such as a purchase. Conversion rate = conversions ÷ visitors.
**Class example:** An organic Instagram post cannot link to a landing page, so you need a paid ad for that. One click to the landing page is one visitor, and conversion is the move from that click to checkout.
**Business example:** Brands put a single link in their Instagram bio, or use link stickers in Stories, because feed posts do not carry clickable links. Paid ads are the main way to send feed viewers straight to a product page.
**Remember:** Traffic, time spent and engagement mean nothing if no money comes in.

### Why traffic does not convert

1. High cart abandonment.
2. No cash-on-delivery option.
3. A checkout page that is not simple.

**Business example:** The Baymard Institute puts average online cart abandonment at about 70%. Amazon's 1-Click ordering, patented in 1999, was built to cut checkout steps.
**Business example:** Flipkart, Myntra and Meesho keep cash on delivery because many Indian shoppers, especially first-time buyers, do not trust paying online upfront.
**Key idea:** The simpler the checkout, the higher the conversion.

### What to track in GA4

**Definition:** GA4 (Google Analytics 4) is Google's current analytics tool. It replaced Universal Analytics in July 2023.
**Class example:** Track cost per order, customer lifetime value (CLV), e-commerce events, and financial metrics from the point of sale onward.
**Formula:** CLV = average order value × purchases per year × years the customer stays (textbook).

## KPIs versus metrics

**Definition:** A KPI is a performance measure linked to a goal. A metric is any number that quantifies something.
**Class example:** Offline conversion rate = buyers ÷ walk-ins. Pull it from the CRM or count manually each week.
**Business example:** A store with 500 walk-ins and 50 buyers has a 10% conversion rate. Retail chains such as Lenskart track store conversion to judge staff and layout.
**Exam tip:** Every KPI is a metric, but not every metric is a KPI. Page views are a metric; conversion rate against a target is a KPI.

## Analysis versus analytics

**Definition:** Analysis turns past and present data into visuals to understand what happened. Analytics uses data to predict what will happen.
**Class example:** Power BI is an analysis tool, not an analytics tool. Analytics 1.0 has moved on; GA4 is the current standard to explore.
**Class example:** In the class case, version 1.0 tracked only logins. Version 2.0 tracked time spent and how users moved from stage to stage.
**Business example:** Netflix uses analytics to predict what you will watch next and to decide which shows to commission.

## Building a dashboard

1. Start with the report.
2. Do the analysis (pivot tables work well).
3. Build the dashboard last.

**Definition:** A dashboard is a visual summary of KPIs that tells a story and points to action.
**Class example:** Use visuals, not tables. Aim for about two KPIs per page. Show where the process falls short and recommend a fix. Compare against a threshold: if conversion was 50% last year, explain why this year differs.
**Exam tip:** A good dashboard answers three questions: what happened, why, and what we do next.

## Dataset exercise: delivery delays

**Class example:** Amazon uploads transactions daily or next day depending on volume. You tested whether delays came from particular delivery staff, warehouses or product types. The dataset was inconsistent, which made cleaning part of the task.
**Business example:** Delhivery and Amazon track delivery performance by hub and courier so they can fix the weakest link rather than guess.
**Remember:** When you prompt AI to analyse data, name the framework you want it to use.

## What the faculty stressed

- Read, interpret, act.
- Engagement without conversion is not success.
- Simplify checkout to lift conversion.
- Dashboards must tell a story and recommend action.

## Practice questions

**Q1.** Differentiate a KPI from a metric with an example.
**A:** A metric is any number, such as page views. A KPI is a metric tied to a goal, such as conversion rate against a 3% target. Every KPI is a metric, but not every metric is a KPI.

**Q2.** Give three reasons why website traffic may not turn into sales.
**A:** High cart abandonment, no cash-on-delivery option, and a complicated checkout page. Average online cart abandonment is about 70%, so simplifying checkout often gives the biggest gain.

**Q3.** Distinguish analysis from analytics.
**A:** Analysis studies past and present data to explain what happened, for example charts in Power BI. Analytics uses data to predict what will happen, such as Netflix predicting what a user will watch next.

**Q4.** A store gets 800 walk-ins and 64 buyers in a week. Calculate and interpret the conversion rate.
**A:** 64 ÷ 800 = 8%. The manager should compare it with past weeks or a target and look at staff, layout or stock if it is falling.

**Q5.** What makes a good dashboard?
**A:** It uses visuals, shows about two KPIs per page, compares results against a threshold, and tells a story that ends in a recommendation. It comes after the report and analysis stages.

**Q6.** Why do Indian e-commerce firms keep cash on delivery?
**A:** Many Indian buyers, especially first-time online shoppers, do not trust paying upfront. Removing COD would raise abandonment, so Flipkart and Myntra keep it to protect conversion.

This D&SMA class traced how web analytics grew from static pages to full interaction tracking, and how companies use that data to retarget buyers and check decisions. It separated predictive from prescriptive analytics, warned against following models blindly, and ended with a pair exercise mapping a buyer's journey with SMART recommendations.

## Key terms

| Term | Meaning | Class example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Web analytics | Collecting and studying website behaviour data | Time on page, filters used |
| Retargeting | Showing ads to people who visited but did not buy | Laptop spec filters followed by ads |
| Funnel | The steps from visit to purchase | Visit, click, add to cart, purchase |
| Predictive analytics | Using past data to forecast what will happen | Forecasting next quarter's sales |
| Prescriptive analytics | Recommending actions to reach a target | What to do to hit 100,000 steps |
| Outcome KPI | The final result a business cares about | Conversion, ROI |
| Customer journey map | A visual of every stage a buyer goes through | Pair exercise on an EV buyer |
| Buyer persona | A profile of a typical buyer | Bengaluru professional |
| SMART | Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound | Required for recommendations |

## How web analytics grew

**Definition:** Web analytics is collecting and studying data on how people use a website.
**Class example:** The web moved from static pages you could only read to sites that record every interaction. The class dated Web Analytics 1.0 to around 2010.
**Business example:** Early analytics read server log files in the 1990s. Google bought Urchin and launched Google Analytics free in 2005, which made tracking standard for most websites. GA4 replaced the older version in 2023.
**Class example:** The workflow: collect data in sheets, upload to a drive, build visuals, then interpret them for the company's need.

## KPIs depend on the role

**Class example:** A social media lead tracks different KPIs from other managers. For e-commerce, track how much customers pay and how often.
**Business example:** A social media lead might track reach, saves and profile visits, while an e-commerce head tracks average order value and repeat purchase rate.

## Tracking behaviour and retargeting

**Definition:** Retargeting shows ads to people who visited a site or app but did not buy.
**Class example:** Apple, Lenovo and Facebook track time on page, products viewed and filters used (such as laptop specs), then retarget you with ads to bring you back.
**Business example:** The Meta Pixel on a brand's website records which products you viewed, so Instagram can later show you that exact product. Google Ads remarketing works the same way across websites and YouTube.

### The funnel

1. Visit.
2. Click.
3. Add to cart.
4. Purchase.

**Key idea:** Your job is to move people from engagement to conversion, and to use data to check whether a management decision was right.

## Predictive versus prescriptive analytics

**Definition:** Predictive analytics uses past data to forecast what will happen. Prescriptive analytics recommends the actions needed to reach a target.
**Class example:** Prescriptive: what to do to hit 100,000 steps.
**Business example:** Netflix predicts what you will watch next (predictive). UPS's ORION system tells each driver the best route to take (prescriptive), and UPS reports it saves about 100 million miles a year.
**Exam tip:** Predictive answers "what will happen?"; prescriptive answers "what should we do?". Give one company example for each.

## Never follow a model blindly

**Class example:** A manager should test the model and the data first, and know who is accountable if it is wrong.
**Business example:** Zillow shut its home-buying business, Zillow Offers, in 2021 after its pricing algorithm overpaid for thousands of houses. The company took losses of over $500 million and cut about a quarter of its staff.
**Remember:** A model is a tool, not a decision-maker. Someone must own the decision.

## Case: "the model says increase ads"

1. Define the outcome KPI and the promised ROI before acting.
2. Past performance is not a KPI for the future.
3. Engagement and interactions are not outcomes. Conversion is the only final outcome.
4. Start with a specific goal before opening a report, so you do not waste time on irrelevant numbers.
5. Win stakeholders with evidence and give specific answers.

**Formula:** ROI = (revenue from the campaign − cost of the campaign) ÷ cost of the campaign × 100 (textbook).
**Business example:** A campaign costing ₹2 lakh that brings ₹5 lakh in sales gives ROI = (5 − 2) ÷ 2 × 100 = 150%.

## Pair exercise: customer journey map

**Definition:** A customer journey map shows each stage a buyer goes through, with their thoughts, pain points and the channels they use.
**Class example:** One partner interviews the other as a buyer, asking about the person, not the product. Products offered: a home loan, an EV (a Mahindra EV at ₹20 to 25 lakh), an online MBA, a 3-day hotel package, or an OTT subscription.

### Steps

1. Build a buyer persona (example: a Bengaluru professional, with age, motives and behaviour).
2. Look at the financial side: what is the risk of lending or selling to this buyer (job security, employment gaps, a past layoff)?
3. Look at the marketing side: which channels lead to discovery, and what drives the decision?
4. Fill a findings table: pain points and confusion, turned into lessons for the company.
5. Output the buyer's risk level, the percentage chance they buy, how to track them and how to convince them, as an infographic plus a decision table.
6. Write at least 5 SMART recommendations per EV category, each tied to a KPI.

**Definition:** SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. George Doran introduced the idea in 1981.
**Business example:** "Raise test-drive bookings from Instagram ads by 20% in 60 days" is SMART; "improve social media" is not.
**Business example:** Tata Motors led India's electric car market for several years with around 70% share in 2023, helped by the Nexon EV and a strong charging-partner network. Your pair leaned towards Tata on past client feedback.
**Remember:** You may write recommendations yourself or with AI; both are accepted.

## What the faculty stressed

- Conversion is the only final outcome.
- Test models before acting on them, and know who is accountable.
- Recommendations must be SMART and tied to a KPI.

## Assignments and deadlines

- Customer journey map pair exercise, practice submission (not graded).

## Practice questions

**Q1.** Differentiate predictive from prescriptive analytics with examples.
**A:** Predictive analytics forecasts what will happen, as Netflix predicts what you will watch. Prescriptive analytics recommends what to do, as UPS's ORION tells drivers the best route, saving about 100 million miles a year.

**Q2.** How does retargeting work? Give an example.
**A:** A tracking tool such as the Meta Pixel records products a visitor viewed. The brand then shows ads for those products on Instagram or Facebook to bring the visitor back to buy.

**Q3.** Why should managers not follow an analytics model blindly? Use Zillow.
**A:** Models can be wrong, and someone must own the decision. Zillow's pricing algorithm overpaid for homes, leading to over $500 million in losses and the closure of Zillow Offers in 2021.

**Q4.** A campaign cost ₹1.5 lakh and generated ₹4.5 lakh in sales. Calculate the ROI.
**A:** ROI = (4.5 − 1.5) ÷ 1.5 × 100 = 200%. The campaign returned twice its cost in profit before other expenses.

**Q5.** Rewrite "improve our EV marketing" as a SMART recommendation.
**A:** "Increase EV test-drive bookings from Instagram ads by 20% within 60 days, measured through booking form submissions." It is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

**Q6.** What are the steps in building a customer journey map?
**A:** Build a buyer persona, assess the financial risk, trace the marketing channels and decision drivers, list pain points in a findings table, estimate risk and purchase probability, and end with SMART recommendations tied to KPIs.

This class focused on building the logic for a website analytics project, specifically the conversion funnel, product detail page evaluation, and how to handle missing data when real company numbers are not available. The discussion moved from AI tool usage for the project to a detailed framework for mapping customer journey from awareness to post-purchase.

## Key terms

| Term | Meaning | Class example |
|---|---|---|
| Awareness | Baseline level of whether a user knows an offering exists | Discussed as the starting point before engagement |
| Engagement | Active interaction and reach that follows awareness | Treated as a key KPI to show the user journey |
| Conversion | The point where a user's need is matched with the right product and a purchase happens | Earphones example, user must find the right product to convert |
| Funnel | A sequence of steps where the number of users reduces at each stage | 1,000 users at engagement, lower number at conversion |
| Product Detail Page (PDP) | The specific product page that drives the final purchase decision | Earbuds example, checked for size, warranty, reviews |
| Social proof | Ratings and reviews that build buyer trust | Volume and quality of reviews tracked on PDP |
| Conversion gap | The share of visitors who do not buy after viewing a product page | Stated as 70 percent non-conversion on PDP visits |
| VIP pattern | Behaviour of high value customers who add to cart repeatedly but do not buy | Used to identify priority customers for targeting |
| Information gap | Missing data that a manager must trace and fill from another source | Social media suggested as a source to fill internal data gaps |
| Ad Library | Facebook's public tool to view live and past ads of any page | Suggested by Santanu Paul to study competitor ads |

## Website Analytics Project Framework

### Website selection and documentation
**Definition:** The first task for the project is to choose one real website and prepare a document analysing it.
**Class example:** Students were told to research and finalise a website before building the funnel analysis.
**Exam tip:** If asked about project methodology, mention that the first step is always website selection followed by documentation of its structure and funnel.

### Awareness vs Engagement vs Conversion
**Definition:** Awareness is simply knowing an offering exists. Engagement is the active interaction that follows. Conversion is the actual completion of the desired action, usually a purchase.
**Class example:** The faculty used the earphones example, saying a web page exists to guide the user to the exact product that fits their need. If the user cannot find the right product, it is a conversion failure, not just a traffic problem.
**Business example:** Amazon India uses personalised recommendation and filter systems on its search and category pages so that a user searching for "wireless earbuds" is guided quickly to a matching product, reducing drop off between engagement and conversion.
**Remember:** Awareness feeds engagement, and engagement only becomes valuable if it ends in conversion.
**Exam tip:** Always present this as a sequence (Awareness → Engagement → Conversion) in diagram form when answering funnel questions.

### Conversion funnel logic
**Definition:** A funnel is a model showing how the number of users keeps reducing as they move through stages from initial reach to final purchase and beyond.
**Class example:** Faculty gave an illustrative number: 1,000 users at the engagement stage falling to a smaller number at conversion, to show the standard decay pattern expected in any funnel.
**Business example:** Flipkart's typical funnel moves from app visits to product views to cart additions to checkout, with each stage showing fewer users than the one before, a pattern e-commerce analysts use to find the weakest stage.
**Formula (textbook):** Conversion rate = (Number of users who convert / Number of users who entered that funnel stage) x 100
**Exam tip:** When asked to build a funnel for a project, always use assumed but logically decreasing numbers since real company data is proprietary and usually unavailable to students.

### Product Evaluation Framework
**Definition:** This framework looks at how a user moves from browsing a broad category to selecting one specific product, and what features of the site help or block this movement.
**Class example:** Three focus areas were named: inventory and discovery (number of products and information shown), interface flexibility (ease of filtering), and category navigation (how users move through categories to reach one product).
**Business example:** Myntra's filter system for size, colour, brand, and price lets a user narrow down thousands of listings to a short, relevant set, which is a direct application of interface flexibility.

### Product Detail Page (PDP) analysis
**Definition:** The PDP is the page for one specific product and is treated as the main driver of conversion once a user has narrowed down their choice.
**Class example:** Key performance areas (KPAs) listed were critical product data (size, warranty), social proof (ratings and reviews), and user engagement (time spent on page).
**Business example:** Boat (the Indian earphones and wearables brand) displays size charts, warranty terms, and thousands of reviews directly on its PDP to reduce the hesitation that causes drop off.
**Remember:** 70 percent of users who visit a PDP do not convert, according to the number given in class. Time spent on the PDP is read as a positive signal of purchase intent, not a negative one.
**Exam tip:** If a question asks why conversion rate is low despite high traffic, use this 70 percent figure and explain it as an evaluation stage drop off, not a traffic problem.

### Information gap analysis
**Definition:** A manager's core job in analytics is to spot where data is missing, understand why it is missing, and identify an alternate source to fill that gap.
**Class example:** Social media was named as a primary alternate source when internal company data is not available to students for the project.
**Business example:** When companies do not share their internal cart or payment data publicly, analysts often use social media engagement data and public ad libraries instead, as was suggested for the Facebook Ad Library.

### Customer profiling by function
**Definition:** The same website data can be read differently depending on which department is using it.
**Class example:** Faculty mentioned Finance and Marketing as two different functional profiles that would look at the same customer and fund investment behaviour differently, along with the idea of segmenting website views by group.
**Business example:** In a company like Zerodha, the Marketing team may look at website visits as leads to convert, while the Finance team looks at the same visits in terms of which investment products or funds are attracting money.

### Data sourcing for the project
**Definition:** Since real company numbers are usually confidential, the project must rely on a mix of assumed numbers and publicly available data types.
**Class example:**
1. Transaction data and preliminary databases were named as sources for metrics.
2. Companies typically do share data on promotions and how they are run.
3. Companies rarely share granular data, such as exact cart contents.
4. VIP or high priority customers can be identified by a behaviour pattern: users who frequently add items to cart but never complete the purchase.
**Business example:** Many D2C brands in India run cart abandonment email or WhatsApp campaigns specifically targeting users who show this add-to-cart-but-no-purchase pattern, treating them as high intent VIP leads.

### Post-purchase experience
**Definition:** The customer journey does not end at the transaction. The post-purchase phase (delivery, support, returns) is part of the overall customer experience that analytics should also track.
**Class example:** Faculty stated this directly while discussing UX strategy for the project, saying the journey continues beyond the sale.
**Business example:** Myntra and Flipkart both track post-purchase metrics like return rate and delivery satisfaction as part of their overall customer experience score, not just the checkout conversion number.

### Ad Library for competitor analysis
**Definition:** The Facebook Ad Library is a free public tool that shows all currently running and past ads of any Facebook or Instagram page, useful for analysing competitor advertising strategy.
**Class example:** Santanu Paul suggested using it to extract data on current ads running for the chosen website or brand. Faculty noted that payment gateway details and similar information cannot be captured through the ad library and need a manual visit to the website itself.
**Business example:** Digital marketers routinely use the Facebook Ad Library to study how competitors like Nykaa or Lenskart position their ad creatives and offers before planning their own campaign.

## What the faculty stressed

- Define every identified "gap" clearly: explain exactly why a piece of data or placement is not matching, rather than noting it vaguely.
- The web page's job is to match the user to the exact product they need. Conversion fails when that match fails, not just when traffic is low.
- Since real company data will not be available for the student project, use logical assumed numbers that still follow the correct funnel decay pattern.
- Time spent on a product detail page should be read as a positive signal of buying intent, an opportunity, not a warning sign.
- Always approach the website analysis from the customer's own journey perspective, including what happens after the purchase is made.
- A manual visit to the actual website is necessary for details like payment gateways, since these cannot be captured by the Ad Library or automated tools.

## Assignments and deadlines

- Select a website and prepare a document analysing it (ongoing initial task, no fixed date given).
- Use the Facebook Ad Library and a manual website visit to gather ad and payment gateway data for the chosen website.
- Build a conversion funnel for the project using assumed but logically decreasing numbers, since real data will not be available.

## Practice questions

**Q1.** Differentiate between awareness, engagement, and conversion as discussed in class, using the earphones example.
**A:** Awareness is simply the user knowing the product or website exists. Engagement is the active browsing and interaction that follows, such as searching or filtering. Conversion happens only when the user finds the exact product matching their need and completes the purchase, as shown in the earphones example where failure to find the right product means conversion has failed even if engagement was high.

**Q2.** Explain the Product Evaluation Framework and its three focus areas.
**A:** This framework tracks how a user narrows down from a broad category to one specific product. The three areas are inventory and discovery (range and information about products available), interface flexibility (how easily a user can filter choices), and category navigation (how users move through categories to reach their target product). Myntra's filter system for size and price is a good real world example of interface flexibility.

**Q3.** What is the significance of the 70 percent figure mentioned for Product Detail Pages?
**A:** It refers to the conversion gap, meaning 70 percent of users who visit a product detail page do not end up buying. Faculty framed this not as a loss but as an opportunity, since the users visiting are already showing intent. Increased time on the page is seen as a positive signal that the user is actively evaluating the product, which analysts can use to design better triggers for conversion.

**Q4.** How should a student handle the lack of real company data while building the funnel for the class project?
**A:** Since actual company numbers are usually proprietary, the project should use assumed numbers that still follow the logical funnel decay pattern, for example 1,000 users at engagement reducing to a smaller number at conversion. Available public data types like promotion details can be used, but granular data like exact cart contents should be estimated rather than expected from the company.

**Q5.** What is a VIP pattern in customer behaviour and how can it be identified?
**A:** A VIP pattern refers to high priority customers identified through a specific behaviour, typically users who repeatedly add items to their cart but never complete the purchase. This pattern signals high interest without conversion, making these users good targets for retargeting campaigns such as cart abandonment offers.

**Q6.** Why is the Facebook Ad Library useful for this project, and what are its limitations?
**A:** The Ad Library lets you see all current and past ads run by a brand's Facebook or Instagram page, which is useful for analysing competitor advertising strategy, as suggested by Santanu Paul. Its limitation is that it cannot show details like payment gateway setup or other on-site operational details, which require a manual visit to the actual website.

**Q7.** Explain why post-purchase experience matters in website analytics, even though the transaction is already complete.
**A:** The customer journey does not stop once the payment is made. Faculty stressed that post-purchase elements like delivery and support are still part of the overall customer experience and should be tracked. Companies that ignore this phase risk losing repeat customers even if their initial conversion numbers look strong.

**Q8.** How do Finance and Marketing teams typically use the same customer data differently, based on the class discussion?
**A:** The same website or transaction data can be read through different functional profiles. A Marketing profile would look at the data to judge lead quality and campaign performance, while a Finance profile would look at the same customer behaviour in terms of fund investment and revenue impact. This shows why segmenting data by department or use case matters in analytics.

This class was a working session on the website analytics project, using GA4 daily data for August and September. You checked whether the available metrics (sessions, checkouts, purchases and revenue) are enough to read the funnel, worked out conversion rate and stage-wise drop-off rate, and mapped the user journey into a three-stage funnel of entry, engagement and conversion. The class also fixed a rounding standard of three decimal places and agreed how to present GA4 channel data and competition analysis in the Excel report.

## Key terms

| Term | Meaning | Class example |
|---|---|---|
| Daily data | Metrics recorded day by day for a website over a period | August and September daily data reviewed in class |
| Session | One visit to the website; in class it was treated as one unique visitor | Used as the base for conversion and drop-off calculations |
| Checkout | The stage where a user begins the payment process after adding items to cart | Checkout counts listed in the daily data; payment gateway drop-off discussed |
| Purchase | A completed order | Purchase counts used as the numerator for conversion rate |
| Revenue | Money earned from completed purchases | Revenue tracked in GA4 and available for download |
| Conversion rate | Share of sessions that end in a purchase | Purchases / sessions x 100; the site's rate was 5.9 percent |
| Drop-off rate | Share of users lost between one funnel stage and the next | First phase drop-off worked out as 30.315 percent |
| Conversion funnel | The stages a user passes through from arrival to purchase | Three stages: entry, engagement, conversion |
| Channel | The source that brings a session to the site (organic search, direct, paid, social and so on) | GA4 Tab 3 filtered to four channels by sessions |
| Rounding standard | Agreed number of decimal places for reporting | All values rounded to three decimal places |

## Purchase and revenue data: validating the metrics

### Reviewing the daily data
**Definition:** Metric validation means checking whether the data you have is complete and suitable for the analysis you want to do, before you start calculating.
**Class example:** The class reviewed the daily data section for August and September. It contained checkouts, purchase counts and revenue values, and the question was whether these metrics are enough to identify where users drop out and how well the site converts.
**Business example:** An Indian D2C brand such as boAt or Mamaearth tracks daily sessions, checkouts, orders and revenue in Google Analytics 4 or Shopify reports. Analysts first confirm that the numbers line up (for example, orders never exceed checkouts) before using them in a funnel report.
**Remember:** Each funnel stage should have fewer users than the stage before it. If a later stage shows a higher number, check the data before you calculate anything.
**Exam tip:** In any analytics answer, state your data period (here, August and September) and list the metrics you used. It shows the examiner your analysis is grounded.

### Session as the base metric
**Definition:** A session is a single visit to the website. In class it was confirmed that, for this project, a session represents one unique visitor.
**Class example:** Santanu Paul asked whether "sessions" meant total visits or unique visitors. The answer was that a session is taken as one unique visitor, so sessions became the base number for all rate calculations.
**Business example:** On Flipkart, one shopper who opens the app in the morning and again at night creates two sessions in Google Analytics, though they are one user. Reports separate "Sessions" from "Users" for this reason.
**Remember:** (textbook) In Google Analytics 4, sessions and users are different metrics. One user can create many sessions. For this project, follow the class convention and treat each session as one visitor, but mention the difference if a theory question asks.
**Exam tip:** Always say clearly what your denominator is. A rate is meaningless if the reader does not know whether it is per session or per user.

## The three-stage conversion funnel

### Funnel structure
**Definition:** A conversion funnel breaks the user journey into stages so you can see how many users move forward and where they leave. The class used three stages.
**Class example:** The faculty described three funnels in the user journey:
- **Entry:** users arriving on the platform.
- **Engagement:** how users interact with the site and discover specific products.
- **Conversion:** the final step that ends in a purchase.
**Business example:** On Nykaa, entry is a visit from an Instagram ad or Google search, engagement is browsing categories, reading reviews and adding to cart, and conversion is the completed payment. Nykaa watches each stage separately because a weak product page and a weak payment page need different fixes.
**Remember:** Entry problems point to traffic quality, engagement problems point to site content and product discovery, and conversion problems point to checkout and payment.
**Exam tip:** When asked to analyse a funnel, name each stage, give its numbers, calculate drop-off between stages, and then suggest one action per weak stage.

### Checkout and payment gateway drop-off
**Definition:** Checkout drop-off is the loss of users between starting checkout and completing the purchase. A large share of it often happens at the payment gateway.
**Class example:** The class looked at checkout conversion and the drop-off at the payment gateway as the last leak in the funnel before purchase.
**Business example:** Indian sites lose many orders to failed UPI or card payments and OTP timeouts. Razorpay and PhonePe promote features such as saved cards, UPI intent flows and one-click checkout (Razorpay Magic Checkout) to reduce this drop-off for merchants.
**Remember:** Checkout to purchase is the stage closest to revenue, so even a small improvement here adds revenue directly.

## Funnel calculations

### Conversion rate
**Definition:** Conversion rate is the percentage of sessions that end in a purchase.
**Formula:** Conversion rate (%) = (Number of purchases / Number of sessions) x 100
**Class example:** Santanu Paul asked what baseline to use for conversion rate. The faculty clarified that you divide purchases by the session number and multiply by 100. The current conversion rate for the site in the project came to **5.9 percent**.
**Business example:** If Nykaa records 2,00,000 sessions in a day and 4,000 orders, its conversion rate is (4,000 / 2,00,000) x 100 = 2 percent. Indian e-commerce sites usually report conversion in the 1 to 3 percent range (textbook), so 5.9 percent would be strong for a typical retail site.
**Remember:** Purchases go on top, sessions go at the bottom. Do not use checkouts as the denominator for overall conversion rate.
**Exam tip:** Show the formula, substitute the numbers, and write the final value to three decimal places, as agreed in class.

### Drop-off rate
**Definition:** Drop-off rate is the percentage of users lost between one stage of the funnel and the next.
**Formula:** Drop-off rate (%) = ((Users at earlier stage − Users at next stage) / Number of sessions) x 100
**Class example:** Santanu Paul explained the method for the first phase: subtract the next stage's number from the earlier stage's number, divide by the number of sessions, and multiply by 100. The drop-off for the first phase came to 30.315 percent.
**Business example:** If Myntra has 1,00,000 sessions and 40,000 of them view a product page, then 60,000 visitors left before reaching a product. The first phase drop-off is (60,000 / 1,00,000) x 100 = 60 percent. Myntra would then test better home page banners or search to reduce this.
**Remember:** (textbook) Many analysts divide by the users at the earlier stage instead of total sessions. That gives stage-to-stage drop-off. Dividing by sessions, as done in class, shows each phase's loss as a share of all visitors, so the phases can be compared on one base.
**Exam tip:** Calculate drop-off for every phase, then name the phase with the highest drop-off as the main problem area and suggest a fix for it.

### Rounding standard
**Definition:** A rounding standard is a fixed rule for how many decimal places you report, so that all figures are consistent.
**Class example:** The class decided that all numerical calculations will be rounded off to three decimal places, which is why the first phase drop-off was reported as 30.315.
**Business example:** Swiggy and Zomato investor reports present conversion and order metrics in a consistent decimal format across quarters so that small changes can be compared.
**Remember:** Round only the final answer. If you round middle steps, the final figure can shift.

## GA4 reporting

### Revenue tracking and data download
**Definition:** GA4 records revenue against purchases and lets you export the underlying report data for your own analysis.
**Class example:** The class confirmed that revenue tracking is available in the GA4 property and that the underlying data can be downloaded for calculations in Excel.
**Business example:** A Shopify-based Indian brand such as The Souled Store can link GA4 e-commerce events so each order's value appears in GA4, then export monthly revenue by channel to Excel or Google Sheets.
**Exam tip:** If a question asks how you would verify a funnel figure, say you would export the GA4 report and recalculate it yourself.

### Channel analysis using sessions
**Definition:** Channel analysis groups sessions by the source that brought users in (for example organic search, direct, paid search, social) so you can compare how each source performs.
**Class example:** The required data sits in Tab 3 of the GA4 dashboard. You filter it to show only four channels, chosen on the basis of session data, and present the KPI charts for those channels. Screenshots of the GA4 charts were chosen over manually retyping the same numbers into a table.
**Business example:** Lenskart compares sessions, conversion rate and revenue from Google paid search, Instagram ads, organic search and direct traffic. If one channel brings many sessions but few purchases, the budget for that channel is reviewed.
**Remember:** Pick channels by session volume first, then compare their conversion rate and revenue. A channel with high traffic and low conversion is a different problem from a channel with low traffic and high conversion.
**Exam tip:** Always pair a traffic metric (sessions) with an outcome metric (conversion rate or revenue) when you compare channels.

### Competition analysis
**Definition:** Competition analysis compares your site's traffic, channels and offer against rival sites to judge relative performance.
**Class example:** The Excel report has to answer a set of competition questions, which are in the file shared earlier, alongside the GA4 data.
**Business example:** Mamaearth tracks how much of its traffic comes from search and social compared with rivals such as Plum and WOW Skin Science, using tools like Similarweb, to decide where to spend on ads.

## What the faculty stressed

- Check that your data (sessions, checkouts, purchases, revenue) is enough for the analysis before you calculate.
- Use sessions as the base for both conversion rate and drop-off rate in this project.
- Conversion rate = purchases / sessions x 100. The project site's rate was 5.9 percent.
- Drop-off for each phase = (earlier stage − next stage) / sessions x 100.
- Read the funnel in three stages: entry, engagement, conversion.
- Round every result to three decimal places.
- Filter GA4 Tab 3 to four channels based on sessions and use the GA4 KPI charts directly.

## Assignments and deadlines

- **Excel report (GA4 data and competition analysis):** due tonight, 8 October 2026. Filter GA4 Tab 3 to the four required channels, take screenshots of the relevant KPI charts, answer the competition questions in the shared file, and submit the screenshots together with the completed Excel file as one submission.
- A table for a submission was also mentioned with Tuesday as a possible timeframe. Confirm the exact date with the faculty.

## Practice questions

**Q1.** Define a session and explain how it differs from a user.
**A:** A session is one visit to a website. In class, a session was treated as one unique visitor for the project. In Google Analytics 4, however, one user can create many sessions, so the two metrics are reported separately. Always state which one you are using as your base.

**Q2.** A website has 50,000 sessions and 1,200 purchases in September. Calculate the conversion rate.
**A:** Conversion rate = (1,200 / 50,000) x 100 = 2.400 percent. Purchases are the numerator and sessions are the denominator, as clarified in class. The answer is rounded to three decimal places.

**Q3.** Explain the three-stage conversion funnel used in class.
**A:** Entry is the stage where users arrive on the platform. Engagement covers how they interact with the site and discover products. Conversion is the final step that ends in a purchase. Measuring each stage separately tells you whether the problem is traffic, site content or checkout.

**Q4.** A site has 20,000 sessions. 13,937 users reach the product page. Find the first phase drop-off.
**A:** Users lost = 20,000 − 13,937 = 6,063. Drop-off = (6,063 / 20,000) x 100 = 30.315 percent. This matches the class figure and shows close to a third of visitors leave before reaching a product.

**Q5.** How would you compare marketing channels in GA4, and why filter by sessions?
**A:** Open the channel report (Tab 3 in the class dashboard), filter to the top channels by sessions, and compare their KPIs such as conversion rate and revenue. Filtering by sessions keeps the focus on channels that bring meaningful traffic. You then judge each channel on what that traffic achieves, not on volume alone.

**Q6.** Why is checkout and payment gateway drop-off important to track?
**A:** It is the last stage before revenue, so every user lost here had already shown strong purchase intent. Failed payments, OTP issues or extra form fields often cause it. Fixing this stage, for example with one-click or UPI checkout, raises conversion rate without needing more traffic.

In the first half you scraped book data (titles, prices, ratings and stock status) from a web page with Python, cleaned it so the numbers behaved like numbers, and planned a dashboard with KPIs and charts. In the second half you set up the YouTube Data API to pull video statistics, used views, likes and comments as social media KPIs, and got the brief for the CA2 project on drop-off identification with sentiment graphs and word clouds.

## Key terms

| Term | Meaning | Class example |
|---|---|---|
| Library | A package of pre-written code you import to get ready-made tools | `import pandas as pd`, `import matplotlib.pyplot as plt` |
| Web scraping | Automatically pulling data out of a web page's HTML | Extracting title, price and stock status of books |

| Data type conversion | Changing text values into numbers so you can calculate | Price stored as text converted to a number |

| Pagination | Splitting records across pages with a fixed number per page | 20 books per page, URL for items 1 to 20 |

| AOV | Average Order Value = revenue / number of orders | Mentioned as a core e-commerce KPI |
| Word cloud | A visual where more frequent words appear bigger | Required in the CA2 dashboard for comment analysis |

## Why this analysis matters: user drop-off

**Definition:** User drop-off is the point where visitors leave a website, app or video before completing a goal such as a purchase, a sign-up or watching to the end.
**Class example:** The class opened by looking at how certain images and page layouts could be causing users to drop off. The same idea came back at the end as the core objective of CA2: identify drop-offs and suggest fixes based on competitor analysis.
**Business example:** E-commerce players like Myntra and Flipkart run A/B tests on product images and page layouts and track where users exit the funnel, so they can fix the pages that lose the most buyers.
**Remember:** Drop-off is found with data, and fixed with design. Analytics tells you *where* users leave; testing and comments tell you *why*.

## Setting up the coding environment

### Google Colab

**Definition:** Google Colab is a free, browser-based Python notebook from Google. You run code in cells without installing anything on your laptop.
**Class example:** You downloaded the Python file shared on Google Classroom, opened colab.google.com (or searched "Google Colab") and uploaded the file into a notebook to start the problem. The YouTube API script was also run in Colab.
**Business example:** Analytics teams at Indian startups often prototype scraping and analysis scripts in Colab or Jupyter before moving them to a scheduled production pipeline.
**Exam tip:** If asked for the steps, write them in order: download file, open Colab, upload file, run the import cell, then supply the URL or video ID.

### Python libraries

**Definition:** A library is a program that holds pre-written lines of code. You must import it into your project to use its functions.
**Class example:** Pandas was imported as `pd` and Matplotlib as `plt`. The short name is an object that gives you access to the library's internal functions, for example `pd.read_csv()` or `plt.bar()`.
**Business example:** Data teams at companies like Swiggy and Zomato use Pandas for cleaning order data and Matplotlib or similar tools for quick charts before building BI dashboards.
**Remember:** Pandas = rows and columns. Matplotlib = charts. Scraping libraries (textbook: `requests` to fetch the page and `BeautifulSoup` to parse the HTML) = collecting the data.

## Web scraping

### Purpose and output

**Definition:** Web scraping is the automated collection of data from web pages. The goal is a clean, structured **CSV file** that you can pre-process and analyse.
**Class example:** After the imports ran successfully, the next step was to give the program a web page URL. The code then works out how much data and how many results that page holds.
**Business example:** Indian price comparison sites like Smartprix track product prices across Amazon.in and Flipkart by collecting listing data repeatedly, then show users price history and the cheapest seller.
**Exam tip:** Always state the end product. In this course, the output of data collection is a CSV file ready for pre-processing.

### The extraction funnel

**Definition:** Extraction follows a funnel: observe the page, capture its structure (the HTML elements and their tags or CSS classes), pull out the raw text, then parse out the specific data points you need.
**Class example:** The faculty called the captured page structure "CST" (likely the HTML/CSS structure of the page, i.e. the DOM tree). From that, the code captured:
- **Text** of each product, the main raw source
- **Price**, isolated from the text
- **Stock availability**, whether the item is in stock

The logic counted how many goods were on the **first page** and printed only the **first five rows** (the head of the data, `df.head()`).
**Business example:** A D2C brand like boAt can monitor competitor listings for price and "out of stock" status to spot when a rival runs short and adjust its own ads or prices.
**Remember:** Text first, then price, then stock. Check your result with `head()` before scraping more pages.

### Pagination

**Definition:** Pagination limits the number of records shown per page, so a large list is split across many pages.
**Class example:** The site showed **20 items per page**. You request a specific URL to get the response for a range, such as items **1 to 20**, then move to the next page URL for the next 20. The first version of the code only scraped page one.
**Business example:** Amazon.in search results and Flipkart category pages are paginated, so any scraper or crawler has to loop through page numbers in the URL to collect the full catalogue.
**Formula:** Number of pages = Total records / Records per page (round up). For example, 1,000 books / 20 per page = 50 pages.
**Exam tip:** Mention that scraping only page one gives a sample, not the full dataset. A loop over page URLs fixes this.

## Data cleaning and pre-processing

### Data type conversion

**Definition:** Scraped values often arrive as text (characters). You must convert them to numbers before you can add, average or sort them.
**Class example:** Prices were stored as characters, so totals such as total purchase amount could not be calculated. The fix was to convert them to normal numbers. Extra unwanted characters (like the currency symbol) were removed first so that only the price remained.
**Business example:** When an Indian retailer pulls prices like "₹1,299" from its website, analysts strip the ₹ sign and comma and store 1299 as a number before computing average selling price.
**Remember:** Strip, then convert. Remove symbols and extra text, then change the data type.

### Normalising the rating column

**Definition:** Normalisation means bringing values into one standard, usable format.
**Class example:** Ratings were scraped as words. You map them to numeric scores: "One" becomes 1, "Two" becomes 2, and so on up to 5. Now the column can be counted, averaged and plotted.
**Business example:** Platforms like Nykaa and Zomato store star ratings as numbers (1 to 5) so they can show average ratings and sort products by rating.
**Exam tip:** Use the phrase "converting categorical text to numerical scores (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)".

### Cleaning in Excel and Power BI

**Definition:** The same transformations can be done without code, using spreadsheet or BI tools.
**Class example:** The faculty said type changes can be handled in **Excel** and **Power BI** as well as in code. Power BI was singled out for string work: extracting **substrings** and **removing specific words** from text. In the spreadsheet route, a value (cell A2) was copied into a single cell to set up a value for plotting and further custom changes.
**Business example:** Many Indian FMCG sales teams clean distributor data in Power Query (inside Excel and Power BI) using steps like "Replace values", "Extract text" and "Change type".
**Remember:** Code is faster for repeat jobs and large data. Excel and Power BI are quicker for one-off cleaning.

### Null values

**Definition:** A null value is a blank or missing entry in a column.
**Class example:** You must check the rating column for blank or null values. Missing data is an important factor in analysis because it can distort averages and counts.
**Business example:** If 30% of products on a marketplace have no rating, an "average rating" chart that ignores them can mislead a category manager.
**Exam tip:** Name the check (`df.isnull().sum()` in Pandas) and say what you will do: drop, fill, or flag the missing rows.

**Class example:** Once you understand the structure of the CSV, you can add more columns to it (for example a numeric rating column or a calculated field). Formulas and specific columns can also be passed to an **API** for further processing.

**Class example:** The class referred to **Average Order Value (AOV)** and **Conversion Rate**, and for the book data, **average price** and **maximum price** (heard as "maximum production").
**Formula:** AOV = Total revenue / Number of orders
**Formula:** Conversion rate = (Number of conversions / Number of visitors) x 100
**Business example:** Quick-commerce firms such as Blinkit and Zepto track AOV closely, because a higher basket value spreads delivery cost and improves unit economics.
**Exam tip:** Always pair a KPI with its formula and a one-line meaning.

**Definition:** A dashboard puts KPIs and charts on one screen so you can read the numbers at a glance.

- KPI cards: **average price** and **maximum price**
- **Top prices in descending order**
- **Rating distribution:** bar graph of the number of books at each rating (1 star, 2 stars, and so on). In the class data, **1-star ratings had the highest number of books**.
- **Price vs rating plot:** a scatter plot to see whether higher price relates to higher rating
- Option to **download the underlying data as CSV**

The workflow: take the URL response, convert it into a DataFrame, generate the dashboard, and offer the CSV for download. The scraped pages themselves act as the data source.
**Business example:** Amazon sellers in India use Seller Central dashboards that show sales, ratings and price data together, with download options for detailed reports.
**Remember:** Bar graph for counts by category, scatter plot for the relationship between two numbers, sorted table for top values.

## Collecting social media data with the YouTube Data API

### What an API does

**Definition:** An API (Application Programming Interface) lets your code ask a platform for data in a structured format, instead of scraping the visible page. You send a request with a key and an ID, and the platform returns fields such as views, likes and comments.
**Class example:** After web scraping, the class switched to the **YouTube Data API**, one of the free APIs Google offers through a cloud project, to pull statistics for a video.
**Business example:** Social media agencies in India pull channel and video statistics through the YouTube Data API into reporting dashboards for brand clients, so they do not have to copy numbers by hand from YouTube Studio.
**Remember:** Scraping reads what the page shows. An API gives you the platform's own data in clean fields, within the limits the platform sets.

### Setting up the API key

**Definition:** An API key is a credential that tells Google which project is making the request.
**Class example:** The steps shown in class:
1. Create a project in Google Cloud. The project is saved in the cloud, not on your laptop.
2. From the menu, enable API services and select the **YouTube Data API**.

**Exam tip:** Write the sequence as: project, enable API, credentials, API key, paste into script. Also say that you should keep the key private.

### Using the video ID

**Definition:** An iterative process where you publish, track KPIs, read feedback and refine the next piece of content.
**Class example:** The recommended workflow was: execute an idea, monitor results through views, likes and comments, then read what people say in the comments to refine the strategy.

The first E&I class, with Prof Vandita Dar, argued that you learn more from failure than success. It used Uber to show seeing a problem differently, James Dyson to show persistence, and product exercises (the iPhone launch, a juice machine, a transport product) to test ideas before money is spent.

## Key terms

| Term | Meaning | Class example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entrepreneur | Someone who starts a venture to solve a problem, taking the risk | Travis Kalanick, Uber |
| Intrapreneur | Someone who acts like a founder inside an existing company | Thinking like a founder as an employee |
| Startup | A new venture bringing real innovation to a market | Uber, Airbnb |
| Execution | Turning an idea into a working business | "Anyone can copy an idea, few can build it" |
| Product-market fit | A product that the right customers want enough to pay for | A good product still needs the right customer |
| Substitute | Another product that meets the same need | Rating a new transport product against alternatives |

## Learning from failure

**Key idea:** Study failure more than success. Big, established companies often fail when they expand into a crowded market with no clear advantage.
**Class example:** A good product is not enough. You must find the right customer.
**Business example:** Starbucks entered Australia in 2000 and in 2008 closed 61 of its 84 stores. Australians already had a strong local cafe culture, so Starbucks had no clear advantage there.
**Exam tip:** In a failure question, name the cause precisely: wrong customer, no advantage, poor timing or weak execution. Then give a company that failed for that reason.

## Intrapreneurship

**Definition:** Intrapreneurship means thinking and acting like a founder inside an existing company, using its resources to build something new.
**Class example:** It matters even if you never start your own firm.
**Business example:** 3M's Post-it Notes came from employees Spencer Silver and Art Fry using company time to develop a weak adhesive into a new product. Gmail began as an internal Google project by engineer Paul Buchheit.

## Case: Uber, seeing things differently

**Definition:** Opportunity recognition is noticing a problem others accept as normal and designing a better way.
**Class example:** Travis Kalanick could not get a cab in Paris even with a credit card in hand. Uber built a simple app to connect riders with drivers, and recruited drivers by asking them to earn in their idle time.
**Business example:** Uber was founded in 2009 by Garrett Camp and Travis Kalanick. In India, Ola started in 2010 and adapted the same idea with auto-rickshaws and cash payment.
**Key idea:** Class debate added that execution matters more than the idea, because an idea can be copied but a working operation is hard to build.

## What stops people starting a business

1. Fear of failing at execution.
2. Doubt about whether the idea is good enough.
3. Difficulty finding customers.
4. Money running out before the business works.
5. The time it takes.
6. The need for family support and a network.

**Remember:** Most of these barriers are about uncertainty and support, not about the idea itself.

## Persistence

**Class example:** James Dyson built thousands of prototypes before his vacuum worked. Money helps, but the drive to keep going is personal.
**Business example:** Dyson made 5,127 prototypes over about five years before the bagless cyclone vacuum worked. Dyson is now a global appliance brand.
**Exam tip:** Use Dyson as the standard example of persistence and iteration.

## What counts as a startup

**Definition:** A startup brings real innovation to a market and aims to grow fast. Opening an ordinary business or continuing a family business is not the same.
**Class example:** MBA Chai Wala was the grey-area example. Anant Ambani, Anand Mahindra and the Adani Group were discussed as corporate, not startup, examples.
**Business example:** Prafull Billore started MBA Chai Wala in 2017 as a tea stall and grew it into a franchise chain. Critics argue it is a strong small business brand rather than a tech startup.

## Product evaluation exercises

### The iPhone launch

**Class example:** In 2007 Steve Jobs presented the iPhone as three products (a touchscreen iPod, a phone and an internet communicator) and repeated the list to build suspense before revealing they were one device.
**Key idea:** How you present a product shapes how people value it.

### The juice machine

**Class example:** A juice machine cost about $700 and raised about $120 million, including from Google Ventures. The juice came in packets, so it did not feel fresh, and the packs looked like IV bags.
**Business example:** This was Juicero, launched in 2016. After Bloomberg reported in 2017 that its packs could be squeezed by hand, the company shut down within months. Heavy funding could not fix a product people did not need.

### The transport product

**Class example:** Students rated a new short-distance transport product: its closest substitute and a fair price.
**Exam tip:** Evaluate any product idea on four questions: the problem, the target customer, the closest substitute and the price the customer would pay.

### Rental models

**Class example:** As hotel demand rises, owners rent out houses and resorts to specific customer groups.
**Business example:** Airbnb began in 2008 when its founders rented air mattresses in their San Francisco flat. It grew into a global platform without owning property.

## What the faculty stressed

- Learn from failure first.
- A good product needs the right customer.
- Execution beats ideas.
- Intrapreneurship matters for every employee.

## Practice questions

**Q1.** Distinguish an entrepreneur from an intrapreneur with examples.
**A:** An entrepreneur starts a new venture and carries the risk, such as Travis Kalanick with Uber. An intrapreneur builds something new inside an existing company, such as the 3M employees who developed Post-it Notes.

**Q2.** What lesson does Juicero teach about funding and product need?
**A:** Juicero raised about $120 million but its packs could be squeezed by hand, so the machine added little value. Funding cannot replace a real customer need, and the company shut down in 2017.

**Q3.** Why did Starbucks struggle in Australia?
**A:** Australia already had a strong local cafe culture, so Starbucks offered no clear advantage. It closed 61 of 84 stores in 2008, showing that expanding into a crowded market without an edge leads to failure.

**Q4.** Explain why execution matters more than the idea, using Uber and Ola.
**A:** The ride-hailing idea was easy to copy, as Ola showed in India. What decided success was execution: building driver supply, local payment options and reliable service. A copied idea with better execution can win locally.

**Q5.** List four questions for evaluating a new product idea.
**A:** What problem does it solve, who exactly is the customer, what is the closest substitute, and what price will the customer pay compared with that substitute?

**Q6.** Why is Dyson a strong example of entrepreneurial persistence?
**A:** James Dyson built 5,127 prototypes over about five years before the bagless vacuum worked. His persistence turned repeated failure into a global brand.

This E&I class covered the skills an entrepreneur needs (networking, sales, self-belief, communication) and read data from the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) on failure rates, fear of failure and why people start businesses in India. It also touched on disruptive versus innovative founders and the realities of self-employment.

## Key terms

| Term | Meaning | Class example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Networking | Building relationships that bring people, money and customers | The first team is not always the final team |
| Disruptive founder | A founder who changes how a market works | Knows exactly what they want |
| GEM | Global Entrepreneurship Monitor, a yearly global study of entrepreneurship | 2025 data discussed in class |
| Fear of failure | The main barrier that stops people starting | GEM finding |
| Exit rate | Share of people who closed or left a business | 4.5% and 2.5% quoted |
| Necessity entrepreneurship | Starting a business because jobs are scarce | Motive split in GEM |
| Opportunity entrepreneurship | Starting a business to make a difference or chase a gap | Motive split in GEM |
| Subsistence self-employment | Working for yourself just to earn a living | Plumbers and gig workers |

## Skills an entrepreneur needs

### 1. Networking

**Definition:** Networking is building relationships that bring you co-founders, investors, customers and advice.
**Class example:** No one builds a startup alone. *The Social Network* shows that the first team is not always the final one. Switch to people who can execute the vision.
**Business example:** Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin's stake was heavily diluted as the company grew and brought in experienced people.

### 2. Sales skills

**Class example:** You need sales skills for two reasons: to win customers and to pitch for funding.
**Business example:** Zomato's founders began by collecting restaurant menus in Delhi by hand and persuading restaurants to list. Selling to both restaurants and investors was part of the job from day one.

### 3. Self-belief

**Key idea:** Confidence keeps a founder going when results are slow.

### 4. Clear communication

**Class example:** A woman founder's case showed that communication was what got her company built.
**Business example:** Falguni Nayar left a senior banking job and started Nykaa at 50 in 2012. Her clear story of making beauty products accessible helped win investors and customers, and Nykaa listed in 2021.

### Disruptive versus innovative founders

**Class example:** Disruptive founders differ from merely innovative ones by knowing exactly what they want. Leaders should be flexible and admit vulnerability, and stakeholders need to be supportive.
**Business example:** Reliance Jio's 2016 launch with free voice calls and very cheap data changed how the whole Indian telecom market worked.
**Exam tip:** Disruption changes how a market works; innovation improves a product within it.

## GEM data

**Definition:** The Global Entrepreneurship Monitor is a yearly international study, started in 1999 by Babson College and London Business School, that surveys adults on starting and running businesses. The transcript heard it as "Global Answer Solution Monitor".
**Class example:** The data splits startups by sector (agriculture, services) and gender, and compares countries.

### Findings discussed

- India's business failure rate is well under half of some established markets. One African country (Angola was named) showed a surprisingly high figure.
- High-income countries and parts of the Middle East (UAE, Saudi Arabia) scored lower on how feasible people find starting a business. India scored positive.
- **Fear of failure is the main barrier.**
- About 30% would start again after a failure or exit. Exit rates were quoted at 4.5% and 2.5%, with team breakups a common cause.
- India, last 3 to 5 years: startup rates quoted as 12% for women and 11% for men (as heard; check against the report).
- On the 1 to 10 favourability scale, 5 and above is positive, and India scored 5+ on the listed factors.

**Remember:** These figures were heard in class through speech-to-text. Check exact numbers against the GEM report before quoting them in an exam.

### Why people start

**Definition:** Necessity entrepreneurship is starting because jobs are scarce. Opportunity entrepreneurship is starting to pursue a gap or make a difference.
**Class example:** Motives split between wanting to make a difference and scarce jobs. Family influence was quoted at "75% plus".
**Business example:** Many Indian family businesses, such as Haldiram's, show how strongly family shapes the decision to start and continue a business.

## Self-employment in India

**Definition:** Subsistence self-employment is working for yourself to earn a basic living, not to build a scalable company.
**Class example:** Gig workers such as plumbers call themselves self-employed because they are on no payroll.
**Business example:** Urban Company lists plumbers, electricians and beauticians as independent service partners. It gives them customers and training, but they remain self-employed.
**Exam tip:** Do not treat all self-employment as entrepreneurship. Separate subsistence work from growth-oriented ventures.

## What the faculty stressed

- Networking, sales, self-belief and communication are core skills.
- Fear of failure is the biggest barrier.
- Read up on women entrepreneurship.

## Assignments and deadlines

- Read up on women entrepreneurship (flagged in class).

**Q1.** Name four skills an entrepreneur needs and give an example for one.
**A:** Networking, sales skills, self-belief and clear communication. Falguni Nayar's clear story about making beauty accessible helped her win investors and customers for Nykaa.

**Q2.** What is the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor, and what did it show about fear of failure?
**A:** GEM is a yearly international survey of entrepreneurship, started in 1999 by Babson College and London Business School. It found fear of failure to be the main barrier that stops people starting businesses.

**Q3.** Distinguish necessity from opportunity entrepreneurship.
**A:** Necessity entrepreneurship happens when jobs are scarce, so people start businesses to earn a living. Opportunity entrepreneurship happens when people see a gap or want to make a difference.

**Q4.** Why are sales skills important for a founder?
**A:** Founders must sell twice: to customers, who bring revenue, and to investors, who bring funding. Zomato's founders sold to restaurants and investors from the start.

**Q5.** Is a self-employed plumber an entrepreneur? Discuss.
**A:** In a broad sense yes, as they work for themselves. But most are subsistence self-employed, earning a living without building a scalable venture. Platforms like Urban Company give them customers, but they remain independent partners.

**Q6.** Differentiate a disruptive founder from an innovative one.
**A:** An innovative founder improves a product within a market; a disruptive founder changes how the market works. Reliance Jio's cheap data in 2016 reshaped Indian telecom as a whole.

This E&I class looked at the entrepreneurial mindset: tolerance for ambiguity, grit, and seeing an entrepreneur as a problem solver. It used stories of Rupert Murdoch, Slack, Kunal Shah and Flipkart's Ekart, debated who counts as an entrepreneur, and set a 350-word go-to-market assignment.

## Key terms

| Term | Meaning | Class example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tolerance for ambiguity | Comfort acting without full information | Google placing people in roles to suit this |
| Grit | Passion and persistence toward long-term goals | Setting ambitious but reachable goals |
| Pivot | Changing a business's direction based on what works | Glitch becoming Slack |
| Serial entrepreneur | Someone who starts several ventures | Kunal Shah |
| Captive logistics | A company running its own delivery arm | Flipkart's Ekart |
| Go-to-market (GTM) plan | How a product will reach and win its first customers | The 350-word assignment |

## Personality and ambiguity

**Definition:** Tolerance for ambiguity is the ability to act and stay calm without full information.
**Class example:** Some people need structure and dislike uncertainty; others tolerate it. Google places people in roles that fit this.
**Business example:** Early-stage startups change plans often. Founders who need certainty tend to struggle in the first years.
**Exam tip:** List tolerance for ambiguity alongside risk-taking and need for achievement when answering on entrepreneurial traits.

## India's changing mindset

**Class example:** India's mindset has shifted since last year. More founders restart after losses. The class asked what share of Indians run a business, and 6% to 10% was guessed.
**Business example:** Byju's rise and fall and Paytm's regulatory troubles did not stop new founders. India remains one of the world's largest startup bases, with over 100 unicorns created by the mid-2020s.

## Grit

**Definition:** Grit is passion and persistence toward long-term goals. Psychologist Angela Duckworth popularised the term.
**Class example:** Keep wanting more, but set goals that are ambitious and still reachable.
**Business example:** Zerodha's Nithin Kamath worked as a trader for years before starting Zerodha in 2010. It grew into one of India's largest stockbrokers without taking outside funding.

## Founder stories

### Rupert Murdoch

**Class example:** Murdoch took over his father's newspaper in his early twenties and built a media empire, including a US news channel Donald Trump favours.
**Business example:** He inherited the Adelaide News in 1952 after his father died, then built News Corp. It came to include Fox News, The Wall Street Journal and The Times.

### Who counts as an entrepreneur?

**Class example:** The class debated Elon Musk, Donald Trump and Virat Kohli. The Uber series mentioned was *Super Pumped*.
**Key idea:** An entrepreneur is a problem solver, and "the improviser is the best".
**Business example:** Virat Kohli is a co-owner of the clothing brand Wrogn and invested in brands such as Digit Insurance. The debate is whether celebrity founders build businesses or lend their names to them.

### Slack came from a failed game

**Definition:** A pivot is changing direction when the original plan is not working but part of it is.
**Class example:** Glitch was a gaming company that built an internal chat tool, which became Slack.
**Business example:** Stewart Butterfield's company Tiny Speck shut down the game Glitch in 2012 and launched Slack in 2014. Salesforce bought Slack in 2021 for about $27.7 billion. Butterfield had pivoted before: Flickr also grew out of an online game.

### Kunal Shah

**Class example:** Kunal Shah's early ventures moved from wire transfers (sold for about 1 million) to mobile value-added services, which smartphones then made obsolete.
**Business example:** He co-founded FreeCharge, which Snapdeal bought in 2015 for about $400 million, then founded CRED in 2018.
**Remember:** Serial entrepreneurs learn from each venture. A business made obsolete by technology can still teach the next one.

### Flipkart's Ekart

**Definition:** Captive logistics means a company runs its own delivery network instead of outsourcing it.
**Class example:** Flipkart's logistics arm is Ekart. Zomato came up on partnerships.
**Business example:** Flipkart built Ekart because third-party couriers could not reliably handle cash-on-delivery and last-mile delivery in India. Owning delivery gave it control over customer experience.

## What the faculty stressed

- Entrepreneurs solve problems and improvise.
- Grit and tolerance for ambiguity separate founders who last.
- Pivots are normal; many big companies started as something else.

## Assignments and deadlines

- Handwritten plan of about 350 words covering go-to-market, marketing, funding and user acquisition, due end of day 11 Sep.

## Practice questions

**Q1.** What is tolerance for ambiguity, and why does it matter for founders?
**A:** It is the ability to act calmly without full information. Early-stage ventures change plans often, so founders who need certainty struggle, while those who tolerate ambiguity can keep deciding and moving.

**Q2.** Explain grit with an Indian business example.
**A:** Grit is passion and persistence toward long-term goals. Nithin Kamath spent years as a trader before starting Zerodha in 2010 and grew it without outside funding into one of India's largest stockbrokers.

**Q3.** What is a pivot? Use Slack.
**A:** A pivot is changing direction when the original plan fails but part of it works. Tiny Speck's game Glitch failed, but its internal chat tool became Slack in 2014, and Salesforce later bought it for about $27.7 billion.

**Q4.** Why did Flipkart build its own logistics arm?
**A:** Third-party couriers could not reliably handle cash on delivery and last-mile delivery in India. Ekart gave Flipkart control over delivery speed and customer experience.

**Q5.** Is a celebrity who starts a brand an entrepreneur? Discuss.
**A:** Yes, if they take real risk and help build the business, as with Virat Kohli's stake in Wrogn. Less so if they only lend their name. The test is whether they solve a problem and carry risk.

**Q6.** Outline what a go-to-market plan should cover.
**A:** The target customer, the value proposition, pricing, channels for reaching customers, the marketing plan, how users will be acquired early, and how the launch will be funded.
