This class was a hands-on session on customer discovery interviews for a student laundry service idea. You learned how to screen respondents against the target segment before talking, how to run the conversation as an interview to understand needs rather than as a sales pitch, and how to read customer engagement. The session ended with an evaluation of team interviews (Manu, Francis and Daniel), which pointed to weak trust-building and pitching too early.

## Key terms

| Term | Meaning | Class example |
|---|---|---|
| Customer discovery interview | A conversation with a potential customer to learn about their problem and behaviour before selling | Interviewing students about their laundry needs |
| Target segment | The specific group of customers the venture is built for | Students, checked by name, age and student status |
| Screening | Checking that a respondent fits the target segment before the interview | Interview stops if the lead does not fit the demographic |
| Customer scenario | The real-life context in which the customer faces the problem | Living in a hostel versus living at home |
| Problem validation | Testing whether customers really have the problem and care about solving it | Asking whether students need a one-day laundry service |
| Product demo | Showing the product to explain what it does | Demo shown to the interviewer, not used as a sales pitch |
| Premature pitching | Selling the product before understanding the customer's need | Teams started pitching too early in the conversation |
| Rapport (trust-building) | The comfort and trust that makes a customer open up | Lack of bonding observed in the evaluated interviews |
| Customer engagement | How much the customer talks, shares and shows interest | Short yes/no answers and low talk time signalled low interest |
| Digging phase | The probing part of the interview where you ask follow-up questions | Teams asked many questions while digging |

## Customer discovery interviews

### Purpose of the interview
**Definition:** A customer discovery interview is a structured conversation with a potential customer to learn about their problem, current behaviour and willingness to pay, before you build or sell. (textbook) This is the first step of Steve Blank's customer development model.
**Class example:** The team planned to approach students and frame the interaction as a survey or interview to understand their needs. A key question was whether students actually require a one-day laundry service.
**Business example:** UClean, the Delhi-based laundry franchise chain, grew by studying how urban households and students handle washing, ironing and turnaround time. Fast turnaround became part of its offer because customers said waiting several days was a pain point.
**Remember:** The goal is to learn, not to sell. You judge success by how much you learn about the customer's problem.
**Exam tip:** (textbook) Mention Rob Fitzpatrick's "The Mom Test": ask about the customer's life and past behaviour, not their opinion of your idea, because people are polite and will praise any idea.

### Interview versus sales pitch
**Definition:** An interview collects information from the customer. A pitch tries to persuade the customer to buy. Mixing the two too early biases the answers.
**Class example:** The class clarified that the product demonstration should be shown to the interviewer (the evaluator), and it should not be treated as a customer sales pitch.
**Business example:** Before scaling, Zomato's founders collected restaurant menus and studied how office workers chose where to eat (Foodiebay stage). They understood the search problem first and only later built paid listings for restaurants.
**Remember:** Talk less, listen more. The customer should do most of the talking.

## Screening and customer profiling

### Verifying the target demographic
**Definition:** Screening means confirming that a respondent belongs to your target segment before you spend time interviewing them. Data from the wrong people misleads you.
**Class example:** The team decided to first check whether a lead fits the target demographic (name, age and student status) before going further. If the person does not match the target segment, the interview does not proceed.
**Business example:** Survey and research firms in India, such as Kantar, use screener questions (age, city, occupation, product usage) at the start of every study and drop respondents who do not qualify.
**Remember:** Ten interviews with the right people beat fifty with random people.
**Exam tip:** When you describe your research method, state your screening criteria clearly. It shows the sample matches the segment.

### Understanding the customer's scenario
**Definition:** The customer scenario is the real situation in which the problem shows up. The same product can matter a lot in one scenario and very little in another.
**Class example:** The team had to find out whether each student lives in a hostel or at home. A hostel student with no washing machine has a stronger laundry problem than a student whose family handles washing at home.
**Business example:** Stanza Living and Zolo bundle laundry into their student and young-professional housing because residents away from home do not have family support or space for a washing machine.
**Remember:** Segment by situation, not just demographics. Two 20-year-old students can have very different needs.

## Reading engagement and evaluating interviews

### Customer engagement signals
**Definition:** Engagement signals show how interested the customer really is: how long they talk, how much detail they share, and whether they ask questions back.
**Class example:** Santanu Paul observed that the customer's share of talk and engagement time were very low, with mostly brief yes/no responses. The customer showed little interest in the offers, so the conversion potential was judged to be low.
**Business example:** (textbook) In startup research, strong signals include a customer describing workarounds they already use, asking when the product will launch, or offering to pre-pay. Dunzo's early growth came from WhatsApp users repeatedly asking for errands to be run, a clear signal of real demand.
**Remember:** Polite yes/no answers are not validation. Look for stories, detail and commitment.
**Exam tip:** If asked how to judge interview quality, mention talk-time ratio, depth of answers and any commitment (time, money or referral) from the customer.

### Evaluation of team interviews (Manu, Francis and Daniel)
**Definition:** Interview evaluation scores how well an interviewer built rapport, probed the problem, collected data and avoided bias.
**Class example:** Santanu Paul reported the scores for Manu, Francis and Daniel against set criteria, with a score of 7.5 mentioned. Their strengths: they asked many questions in the digging phase and collected the business data they needed. Their weaknesses:
- Customers were not very responsive.
- There was little trust or bonding in the conversation.
- One customer dominated while the other stayed silent.
- They started pitching too early and moved away from the customer's specific needs.
**Business example:** Amazon's "Working Backwards" approach starts every new product from the customer's problem and writes a press release and FAQ around that need before building. Pitching features first would go against this.
**Remember:** Build trust first, dig into the problem next, and show the product last, if at all.

### Trust-building in interviews
**Definition:** Trust-building (rapport) is creating comfort so the customer shares honest information. Without it, answers stay short and guarded.
**Class example:** The lack of trust and bonding was the main reason customers in the evaluated interviews gave little response.
**Business example:** Meesho trained its resellers to sell through friends and family on WhatsApp because buyers trusted people they already knew. Trust moved the conversation forward faster than any product pitch.
**Remember:** In group interviews, draw in the silent person directly by name so one voice does not dominate the data.
**Exam tip:** Name practical rapport steps: introduce yourself and the purpose, start with easy questions about their routine, listen actively, and summarise what they said back to them.

## What the faculty stressed

- Screen first: check name, age and student status, and stop if the person is outside the target segment.
- Understand the customer's scenario (hostel or home) before judging the need.
- Treat the conversation as an interview to learn needs, not a sales pitch. The demo is for the interviewer.
- Test the specific need, such as whether students want one-day laundry service.
- Short yes/no answers and low engagement mean low conversion potential.
- Build trust before digging, and do not pitch too early.
- Manage group interviews so one customer does not dominate.

## Practice questions

**Q1.** What is a customer discovery interview and how is it different from a sales pitch?
**A:** It is a conversation to understand a potential customer's problem, context and behaviour before you sell. A sales pitch tries to persuade the customer to buy. If you pitch too early, the customer reacts to your product instead of describing their real problem, so the data becomes biased.

**Q2.** Why should you screen respondents before an interview? Give the criteria used in class.
**A:** Screening makes sure you collect data only from people in your target segment, so your conclusions apply to the right customers. In class, the team checked name, age and student status. If the respondent did not match the segment, the interview did not continue.

**Q3.** For a one-day laundry service aimed at students, why does the customer's living scenario matter?
**A:** A student in a hostel usually has no washing machine and no family support, so the need for quick laundry is strong. A student living at home may have the work done by family and feel little need. Knowing the scenario helps you segment correctly and judge real demand.

**Q4.** List the signals that tell you a customer is not engaged in an interview.
**A:** Short yes/no answers, low talk time, little detail about their own experience and no interest in offers are all weak signals. In class, these signs led to the conclusion that conversion potential was low. Strong signals would be stories of current workarounds, follow-up questions or a willingness to commit.

**Q5.** Based on the class evaluation of Manu, Francis and Daniel, what went wrong and how would you fix it?
**A:** They asked many questions and gathered the business data, but there was little trust, one customer dominated, and they pitched too early. You would fix this by building rapport at the start, involving every participant by name, and holding back the product until the problem is fully understood.

**Q6.** Explain the "Mom Test" and how it applies to customer interviews. (textbook)
**A:** Rob Fitzpatrick's Mom Test says you should ask about the customer's life and past behaviour, not whether they like your idea, because people give polite but false praise. For the laundry idea, ask "How did you get your clothes washed last week?" instead of "Would you use our service?". Facts about past behaviour are far more reliable than opinions about the future.

This first IMC day set up how Prof Sachin Sinha runs the course: few slides, lots of ad dissection, and weekly in-class exercises. You worked through a self-discovery sheet, learned lateral thinking through famous ads, separated income from standard of living, and closed with a consumer behaviour quiz and an AI persona task.

## Key terms

| Term | Meaning | Class example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Critical appreciation of ads | Dissecting an ad the way you would analyse a poem: headline, visual, idea, audience | Collecting ad specimens in the class WhatsApp group |
| Johari Window | Four-pane model of what you and others know about you | Part C, the hidden self you wrote on the P&C sheet |
| Lateral thinking | Solving a problem sideways, by changing the angle instead of pushing the obvious logic | Avis turning "No. 2" into a promise |
| Income | Personal, invisible, cognitive measure of what you earn | Salary, bank balance |
| Standard of living (SOL) | Social, visible, behavioural display of how you live | House, car, clothes, phone |
| Conspicuous consumption | Buying luxury mainly to show you can afford it | Visible logos and flagship phones |
| Homeostasis | The drive to close the gap between your current and desired state | Hunger pushing you to eat |
| Sociogenic need | A need created by society or peers | Wanting the phone your friends carry |
| Persona | A semi-fictional profile of one type of consumer (Latin for "mask") | Your AI-made consumer portrait |

## How the course works

- Classes run mostly on Mondays in three blocks: 8:30 to 10:00, 10:30 to 12:00 and 2:45 to 4:15.
- Few plain slides, no 15 to 20 page cases. Laptops and ChatGPT are allowed.
- CIA 1 and CIA 3 happen in class. Class participation carries 15 marks for speaking up.
- Start collecting print and digital ads now. The course is built on critiquing them.

**Exam tip:** In any IMC answer, analyse an ad in the same order every time: target audience, big idea, headline, visual, call to action, then what the brand wanted you to feel.

## Self-discovery and the Johari Window

### The P&C sheet

The sheet (P&C means Private and Confidential) asked for your name story, a 2030 vision (where you will live, what work you will do, your personal life), a mania and a phobia, a role model, the person you value most, your greatest expectation from life and your biggest regret.

**Remember:** A mania is a harmless, irrational action you repeat often and others notice. A phobia is an irrational fear. The faculty said everyone has both.

### Johari Window

**Definition:** A model by Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham (1955) that splits self-knowledge into four panes: Open (known to you and others), Blind (known to others, not you), Hidden (known to you only) and Unknown (known to no one until something triggers it).
**Class example:** You wrote Part C, the hidden self, including one negative trait. The film *Secret Superstar* was used to show a hidden talent that surfaces only when triggered.
**Business example:** Brands use the same idea in research. Unilever's Dove "Real Beauty Sketches" (2013) showed that women described themselves far more harshly than strangers did, a "blind" gap the campaign then spoke to.
**Exam tip:** Link the Johari Window to consumer research: focus groups surface the Open pane, while projective techniques and observation reach the Blind and Hidden panes.

## Lateral thinking in advertising

**Definition:** Lateral thinking, a term coined by Edward de Bono, means solving a problem by changing the angle of approach instead of following the obvious step-by-step logic. Linear thinking fails in imaginative tests such as JEE Advanced or CAT.
**Class example:** Lateral inversion (a mirror image) shows how perspective changes what you see. "A hen is just an egg's way of making another egg."

### Ads discussed in class

1. **Sleepwell:** "Did you sleep well?" ties the brand name to the benefit without listing features or price.
2. **Cadbury 5 Star, "Do Nothing":** celebrates doing nothing, the opposite of what chocolate ads usually promise.
3. **Avis, "We're No. 2, so we try harder":** turns second place into a promise of better service.
4. **"Smoking reduces weight":** dark humour, because the weight you lose is your lungs.

**Business example:** Avis ran "We try harder" from 1962 with agency DDB. The company had been losing money for years and turned profitable within about a year of the campaign, and the line stayed in use for decades.
**Business example:** Amul's topical ads with the Amul girl, running since 1966, use lateral wordplay on current news every week. The brand gets huge recall on a small budget because each ad is a fresh angle on something people already talk about.

### Puzzles used in class

- Write "under" below "arrest" to show "under arrest".
- The surgeon who says "I can't operate, he's my son" is the boy's mother. The puzzle exposes gender bias.
- Decoding "convincing" from clues about gerunds and "12 on 15" (C on G).

**Remember:** You are a marketer for about 9 hours a day and a consumer for the other 15. Bring the consumer side into your work.

## Income versus standard of living

**Definition:** Income is personal, cognitive and invisible. Standard of living is social, behavioural and visible. The split maps to the ABC model of attitude: Affective (feel), Behavioural (do), Cognitive (know).
**Class example:** The Nawab of Lucknow who, though poor, still dressed in full regalia, carrying groundnuts in one pocket for himself and cashews in the other for guests.
**Key idea:** Marketing delivers a standard of living to society. Advertising shows that standard and makes people aspire to it.
**Business example:** Apple sells iPhones in India with no-cost EMI offers through bank partners. The monthly instalment lets a buyer display a premium standard of living that their income alone could not pay for upfront.
**Exam tip:** When a question asks why aspirational ads work, use the income versus SOL split: ads sell the visible SOL, and finance options close the gap with invisible income.

## Consumer behaviour concepts (Lecture 3 quiz)

### Brain and involvement

**Definition:** The right brain was described as the stronger but passive side, which takes in ads without effort.
**Business example:** Herbert Krugman's research on television (1965) found that people learn from TV ads with very low involvement. This is why brands like Fevicol rely on memorable, humorous visuals rather than arguments.

### Needs and motives

**Definition:** Homeostasis is the drive to balance your current state with your desired state. Sociogenic needs come from society or peers; psychogenic needs are the other, inner ones.
**Class example:** Hunger creates a gap that pushes you to eat.
**Business example:** Snickers' "You're not you when you're hungry" campaign (from 2010) sells a fix for exactly that gap between hungry and normal.

### Conspicuous consumption

**Definition:** Buying luxury to show others you can afford it. Economist Thorstein Veblen coined the term in 1899.
**Business example:** Large visible logos on brands such as Louis Vuitton and Gucci exist partly for this reason. The logo is the product's social signal.

### Personality determinants

**Definition:** Pre-natal determinants of personality form before birth. An ectomorph has a lean, thin build.

## The persona task

**Definition:** A persona (from the Latin for "mask") is a semi-fictional profile of one type of consumer: likes, dislikes, habits and how simple or complex their life is.
**Class example:** You made an AI or real image of yourself as a consumer, titled it with an adjective starting with your first letter, and posted it by 3:50 pm. Feedback on the drafts said to make the tone quirky and authentic, add shades of grey rather than a perfect picture, and use genuine adjectives.
**Remember:** Do not write "Gen Z consumer". Refine your AI prompt several times instead of accepting the first result.
**Business example:** Marketing teams build personas before planning campaigns. Software company HubSpot offers a free "Make My Persona" tool because a campaign aimed at one clear person is easier to write than one aimed at everyone.

## What the faculty stressed

- Critique ads the way you critique poems. Start collecting specimens now.
- Know yourself before you try to understand consumers.
- Lateral thinking beats linear thinking in advertising.
- Income is invisible; standard of living is what advertising sells.
- Iterate your AI prompts. First outputs are rarely good enough.

## Assignments and deadlines

- Consumer persona image posted to the class WhatsApp group by 3:50 pm, 7 Sep.
- Keep collecting ad specimens through the term.

## Practice questions

**Q1.** Explain the four panes of the Johari Window and link each to a consumer research method.
**A:** The Open pane is what you and others know, reached through surveys and focus groups. The Blind pane is what others see but you do not, reached through observation. The Hidden pane is what you know but keep private, reached through anonymous or projective techniques. The Unknown pane surfaces only through triggers, such as in-depth interviews or experiments.

**Q2.** Using the Avis campaign, explain lateral thinking in advertising.
**A:** Linear logic says a brand should hide that it is second. Avis flipped the weakness into a promise: being No. 2 means it must try harder. The new angle made a negative fact the reason to choose the brand, which is lateral thinking.

**Q3.** Distinguish income from standard of living and explain why advertising focuses on the latter.
**A:** Income is personal, invisible and cognitive, such as salary. Standard of living is social, visible and behavioural, such as the car you drive. Advertising sells the visible standard because that is what people aspire to and display, and credit options like EMI close the gap with income.

**Q4.** What is conspicuous consumption? Give one brand example.
**A:** It is buying luxury goods mainly to show others you can afford them, a term from Thorstein Veblen. Louis Vuitton's visible monogram works as a social signal, so part of what the buyer pays for is being seen.

**Q5.** Define homeostasis and show how a brand uses it.
**A:** Homeostasis is the drive to close the gap between your current state and your desired state. Snickers frames hunger as that gap in "You're not you when you're hungry" and offers the bar as the way back to normal.

**Q6.** Why should a marketer build a consumer persona, and what mistakes should be avoided?
**A:** A persona gives the team one clear person to write for, which sharpens message and channel choices. Avoid vague labels like "Gen Z consumer", include real contradictions and dislikes, and refine the profile several times rather than accepting a first draft.

This IMC Monday built the communication model from the ground up: how a message is encoded, carried and decoded, why it gets distorted, and what that means for advertising. Exercises on script direction, The telephone game and an instruction sheet made the point, followed by noise, repetition, roadblock buying, fields of experience, barriers, persuasion and the 1972 Usha ad used for CIA 1.

## Key terms

| Term | Meaning | Class example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Encoding | Turning a thought into a message | Writing an ad headline |
| Decoding | The receiver interpreting the message | Reading the ad |
| Medium | What carries the message | Air carries sound; no sound in a vacuum |
| Noise | Anything that distorts or blocks the message | Fest rehearsals, thinking about lunch |
| Feedback | The receiver's later reaction, collected by the sender | Sales after a campaign |
| Response | The immediate reaction | People leaving a cinema |
| Field of experience | The background that shapes how each person reads a message | Snapchat versus Instagram overlap |
| Roadblock | Same ad on all major channels at the same time | Prime-time 7 to 9 pm |
| Persuasiveness | The sender's power to influence | Speaker skill |
| Persuasibility | How easily the receiver is influenced | Audience openness |

## Parts of a print ad

1. **Headline:** the hook.
2. **Illustration:** the visual.
3. **Copy:** the whole layout.
4. **Body copy:** the product text (the KFC ad had none).

**Class example:** KFC's "Succumb to the crumb" plays on "bread crumb". Cutting a word made it sharper, and the silent b rhymes. Clients want safety and fear being too clever; copywriters want freedom and trust the audience to fill gaps.
**Business example:** Fevicol's ads by Ogilvy, such as the overcrowded bus held together by Fevicol, use almost no words. The visual carries the whole message.
**Exam tip:** When analysing a print ad, name all four parts and say what each does.

## The communication model

**Definition:** Communication is a sender encoding a message, a medium carrying it, and a receiver decoding it. This builds on the Shannon and Weaver model (1949), which added noise as the thing that distorts the signal (textbook).
**Class example:** Air carries sound; there is no sound in a vacuum. Interpretation is decoding.
**Remember:** The law of communication: communication fails, except by chance.

### Hearing versus listening

**Definition:** Hearing is sound reaching the eardrum. Listening is active attention to meaning.

### Encoding versus encryption

**Definition:** Encoding is any conversion of a message into a form. Encryption is encoding for a chosen audience only, such as Morse code or binary.

### Intrapersonal communication

**Definition:** Communication where sender and receiver are the same person.
**Class example:** Thinking is talking to yourself; overthinking is over-talking to yourself. A soliloquy is a character thinking aloud. In dreaming the subconscious sends and the conscious receives; in praying, the reverse.

### Match your language to your audience

**Class example:** A US plumber asked whether hydrochloric acid clears drains. The Bureau of Standards replied in jargon, which he read as a yes. The final reply: "Don't use hydrochloric acid. It eats the hell out of pipes."
**Business example:** Zomato's push notifications and social posts use casual, meme-style language because its young audience decodes that tone instantly.

## Why messages get distorted

### Script direction

**Class example:** A three-panel soft drink billboard (hot man, drinks, relieved) was read right to left in the Gulf, so readers saw relief, then the drink, then distress. English readers scan in a Z-pattern.
**Remember:** Language is not script. English uses Roman script; Hindi, Sanskrit and Marathi use Devanagari; Punjabi uses Gurmukhi; Urdu reads right to left.
**Business example:** Global brands adapt ad layouts for Arabic markets for this reason. The billboard story is a widely told marketing anecdote, so use it as an illustration rather than a verified case.

### The telephone game

**Class example:** "The little boy carried a bright yellow umbrella to school on a rainy morning" came out as "Little boy carried a water bottle to school." Mass messages always get distorted.

### The instruction sheet

**Class example:** The first line said to read everything and do nothing until item 20. Of 42 students, only Saurav came close, and he still wrote his name and address.
**Key idea:** People skim. Put the most important instruction where it cannot be missed.

### The Mandela effect

**Definition:** Many people sharing the same false memory. The term was coined by Fiona Broome in 2009.
**Class example:** India has no national language and no official national game. It is "Maggi" with no "e", and "Thums Up" with no "b".

## Noise, repetition and media buying

### Response versus feedback

**Definition:** Response is the immediate reaction; feedback comes later and is collected by the sender.
**Class example:** A reporter interviewing people leaving a cinema captures response.

### Noise

**Definition:** Noise is anything that distorts or blocks a message. Physical noise includes law students on break and fest rehearsals. Mental noise includes thinking about lunch or placements in class.
**Class example:** At an IIT Kanpur workshop the faculty learned that only about 10% of a class listens at any moment, so each point needs about 10 repetitions.

### Repetition and herd behaviour

**Class example:** If one sheep jumps a barbed-wire fence at one spot, the other 99 follow at the same spot. Each ad exposure is a sheep leaving a bit of wool on the fence, and some always sticks.
**Business example:** Cricket broadcasts repeat the same ads many times in one match. Brands such as Dream11 buy heavy IPL frequency because recall builds with repetition.
**Remember:** Advertising is iterative because audiences rarely take in a message the first time.

### Roadblock advertising

**Definition:** A roadblock places the same ad on all major channels in the same time slot, so switching channels shows the same ad.
**Class example:** Star Plus, Sony, Colors and Zee, 7 to 9 pm.
**Business example:** Brands launching big products in India, such as new smartphones, often buy roadblocks during prime time or across IPL broadcasts and streaming.

### TRP versus IMDb

**Definition:** TRP (television rating point), measured in India by BARC, shows how many people watch. An IMDb rating shows how highly viewers rate quality.
**Class example:** *Anupamaa* has high TRP and a low IMDb rating, and its audience is wider than people assume.
**Exam tip:** Media planners buy on reach (TRP), not on critics' ratings.

### Communication synergy

**Definition:** Using the same star or theme across a show and the ads in its breaks so each supports the other.
**Class example:** Bhuvan Bam in ads during his own series; Shah Rukh Khan ads during a Shah Rukh Khan film.
**Business example:** Bhuvan Bam's series *Taaza Khabar* streamed on Disney+ Hotstar in 2023 (the class said Prime), and brands featuring him gained from the overlap.

## Fields of experience, cohorts and barriers

**Definition:** Communication works in proportion to the overlap between sender's and receiver's fields of experience. This idea comes from Wilbur Schramm's model (textbook).
**Class example:** The faculty does not use Snapchat, so there is no overlap there, but both sides use Instagram.
**Definition:** A cohort shares experiences, not necessarily an age.
**Class example:** Partition, the Mandal agitation (1990), the JP movement (1970s), Anna Hazare (2011), 26/11 and COVID-19.

### Four barriers

1. **Physical:** noise, line static, a voice too soft or too loud.
2. **Semantic:** word meaning, pronunciation, generational slang (Gen X gets ignored in Boomer, Millennial and Gen Z talk).
3. **Cultural:** the West is direct; India, Japan and China are indirect.
4. **Psychological:** feeling overwhelmed, or an inferiority or superiority complex.

**Business example:** KFC's "finger-lickin' good" was reportedly translated in China as "eat your fingers off", a semantic barrier often quoted in marketing classes.

### Persuasion

**Definition:** Persuasiveness is the sender's power to influence. Persuasibility is how easily the receiver is influenced.
**Class example:** The faculty warned against motivational speakers and MLM schemes, which target high persuasibility.

## The Usha ad and CIA 1

**Class example:** The 1972 Usha sewing machine ad by Grant Advertising shows a mother and daughter, both educated and happy, with stereotypes typical of the time. The class compared it to Burger King's "women belong in the kitchen" ad.
**Business example:** Burger King UK tweeted "Women belong in the kitchen" on International Women's Day 2021 to promote a scholarship for women chefs. The joke drew heavy backlash, and the brand apologised and deleted the tweet.

## What the faculty stressed

- Communication fails except by chance, so repeat and simplify.
- Match language to the audience's field of experience.
- Know the four barriers with examples.
- Extroversion is a professional necessity; speak up for your 15 participation marks.

## Assignments and deadlines

- Join the IMC Google Classroom; CIA 1 is submitted there.
- In-class group assignment on the 1972 Usha ad (AI allowed), starting Monday 28 Sep.
- Read up on the 1990 Mandal agitation and the 1970s JP movement.

## Practice questions

**Q1.** Explain the communication model and the role of noise, with an advertising example.
**A:** A sender encodes a message, a medium carries it and a receiver decodes it. Noise, physical or mental, distorts the message along the way. Advertisers repeat messages, as in cricket broadcasts, because noise means most people miss the first exposure.

**Q2.** What is roadblock advertising and when would you use it?
**A:** A roadblock places the same ad on all major channels in the same slot, so viewers cannot escape it by switching. It suits big launches that need maximum reach in a short time, such as a prime-time slot across Star Plus, Sony, Colors and Zee.

**Q3.** List the four barriers to communication with an example of each.
**A:** Physical (a noisy classroom), semantic (slang or a poor translation), cultural (direct Western versus indirect Asian styles) and psychological (feeling overwhelmed by a senior person).

**Q4.** Differentiate TRP from an IMDb rating, and explain which a media planner uses.
**A:** TRP measures how many people watch; IMDb measures how viewers rate quality. Media planners buy on TRP because reach drives ad exposure. *Anupamaa* shows high TRP with a low IMDb rating.

**Q5.** What does the Burger King Women's Day tweet teach about communication?
**A:** The brand encoded a joke leading to a scholarship message, but many readers decoded only the sexist first line. Without shared context the message failed, and the brand had to apologise.

**Q6.** Explain field of experience with an example.
**A:** Communication works only where sender and receiver share background. A message on Snapchat reaches no one who does not use it, while Instagram gives overlap, so the brand should communicate there.

This class covered the building blocks of advertisement design (copy, body copy, illustrations, brand elements), the ATL/BTL/TTL classification of marketing communication, and the three-stage silent communication sequence between product and customer. It also covered important names in Indian and global advertising history for midterm preparation, a case discussion on marketing jewelry to children, and full details of the CIA 1 group assignment on reimagining the Usha sewing machine ad.

## Key terms

| Term | Meaning | Class example |
|---|---|---|
| Copy | The entire layout and everything shown to the client before media release | A minimalistic ad with white space and no body copy is still called "copy" |
| Body copy | The actual text written within an advertisement | Distinguished from the overall ad layout |
| Illustration | Pictorial (non-word) element of an ad | Photographs, cartoons, drawings, AI-generated images |
| Slogan (idea house) | Umbrella term for taglines, punch lines, bylines, ad lines | Usha's "Can't buy better" |
| ATL (Above the Line) | Mass media, broad-reach advertising | TV, print, generally regulated channels |
| BTL (Below the Line) | Targeted, direct communication | Direct marketing, in-store promotions |
| TTL (Through the Line) | Combination of ATL and BTL strategies | Integrated campaigns using both mass and targeted media |
| Silent communication | Non-verbal interaction between product and buyer before purchase | Visual then tactile then performance stages in a garment store |
| Visual communication | First stage: product's look attracts the eye | Being drawn to a shirt's color and design |
| Tactile communication | Second stage: touch and feel assessment | Touching fabric to check quality |
| Performance communication | Third stage: product's function or fit in use | Trying on clothes to check fit |
| Creative brief | Foundation document guiding an ad campaign's creative direction | Used as the base for the CIA assignment |
| Advertising campaign | A series of ads sharing a common theme, usually tied by a slogan | "Thanda matlab Coca-Cola" campaign |

## Advertising Fundamentals: Copy, Illustrations, and Brand Elements

### Copy vs body copy
**Definition:** Copy is everything in the ad layout shown to the client before it goes to media, while body copy is only the written text within the ad.
**Class example:** A minimalistic ad can have heavy white space and no body copy at all, but the layout itself is still called copy.
**Business example:** Fevicol print ads often use minimal body copy but rely on a strong visual, yet the whole print layout is still "copy" in advertising terms.

### Illustrations
**Definition:** Illustrations are the pictorial, non-verbal elements of an advertisement.
**Class example:** Photographs, cartoons, drawings, and AI-generated images were all given as valid illustration types.
**Business example:** Amul's cartoon mascot in its topical ads is a classic Indian illustration-led campaign.

### Essential brand elements
**Definition:** Illustrations and taglines are optional in an ad, but the brand name and logo must always be present.
**Class example:** A brand was discussed where the name and logo are one and the same, with no separate symbol attached.
**Business example:** Coca-Cola's script logo is both its name and its visual identity, similar to the example discussed in class.
**Remember:** Brand name and logo are non-negotiable in any ad; everything else is flexible.

## CIA 1 Assignment: Usha Ad Reimagining

**Decision:** The assignment is a group task and must be a static poster, not a video.

**Groups formed by faculty (not by student choice, to change group dynamics):**
1. Team 1: Keshav, Kushal, Indra
2. Team 2: Ayan, Tanya, Medini, Sushmita
3. Team 3: Nandana, Mallika, Santanu, Rakshita
4. Team 4: Shreya, Sourabh, Harsh

**Brief:** Reimagine an Usha sewing machine ad from a 2026 perspective.

**Fixed constraints (cannot change):**
1. Brand name must remain Usha.
2. Product must remain a sewing machine (newer models allowed).
3. Punchline must remain "Can't buy better".

- Headline, body copy, and illustrations can be fully redesigned.

**Exam tip:** If asked to define a creative brief, use this assignment as your example: fixed brand elements plus creative freedom in execution is exactly how a real client brief works.

## Advertising Icons and Industry History

### David Ogilvy and global pioneers
**Definition:** David Ogilvy is considered a foundational figure of global advertising and founder of the Ogilvy agency.
**Class example:** His book "Ogilvy on Advertising" was recommended as library reading for exam preparation.
**Business example:** Ogilvy agency in India has handled major campaigns for brands like Cadbury and Fevicol.
**Remember:** Other global names mentioned: J. Walter Thompson (JWT) as a major agency, and David Aaker as a leading branding and marketing expert.

### Indian advertising legends
**Definition:** "Ad men" is the general term for advertising professionals, used regardless of gender.
**Class example (faculty-given facts):**
- Alyque Padamsee (misheard as "Ali Padamsee") is called the father of Indian advertising, associated with agency Lintas.
- Piyush Pandey is a legendary figure at Ogilvy, known for iconic Cadbury ads. His sister is singer-actress Ila Arun and his brother Prasoon Pandey is also an ad man. He wrote the autobiography "Pandemonium" with a foreword by Amitabh Bachchan.
- Prasoon Joshi is a lyricist and advertising professional with an MBA in marketing from IMT Ghaziabad. He has headed the CBFC and currently chairs Prasar Bharati. He created "Thanda Matlab Coca-Cola" for McCann Erickson and the "Unbox" campaign.
**Business example:** Cadbury's "Kuch Khaas Hai" and Coca-Cola's "Thanda Matlab Coca-Cola" are real, well-known campaigns tied to these names.
**Exam tip:** Be ready to match name to agency to campaign; this is a likely short-answer question.

### Crossover between advertising and filmmaking
**Definition:** Several Indian advertising professionals moved into mainstream filmmaking.
**Class example:** R. Balki (ad man turned filmmaker) directed "Paa" and "Padman." His wife Gauri Shinde, also from advertising, directed "English Vinglish." Usha Bhandarkar was also mentioned as a notable industry name.
**Business example:** R. Balki's advertising background is often cited to explain the strong tagline-driven storytelling in his films.

## Marketing Communication Frameworks: ATL, BTL, TTL

**Definition:**
1. ATL (Above the Line): mass media, broad-reach, often government-regulated advertising channels like TV and print.
2. BTL (Below the Line): targeted, direct communication methods aimed at specific consumer groups.
3. TTL (Through the Line): a combined strategy using both ATL and BTL together.

**Class example:** These three were defined as the core categories of product and marketing communication.
**Business example:** Hindustan Unilever uses ATL television ads for mass brand building (like Surf Excel) alongside BTL activities such as in-store sampling, making it a TTL strategy overall.
**Exam tip:** Always define all three together in a comparative table if asked; examiners like to see the contrast.

## Silent Communication Framework

**Definition:** Silent communication is the non-verbal interaction between a product and a potential buyer, occurring in a fixed three-step sequence before a purchase decision is made.

**Steps (must follow this order):**
1. Visual communication: the product's look, such as brand, color, and design, attracts the customer's eyes.
2. Tactile communication: the customer touches and feels the product to assess quality.
3. Performance communication: the customer checks how the product actually functions or looks in use.

**Class example:** In a garment store, a customer is first drawn to a shirt by its color and design (visual), then touches the fabric to check quality (tactile), then tries it on to check fit (performance).

**Business example:** Zara stores are designed for this exact sequence, encouraging customers to see, touch, and try garments in-store before buying.

### E-commerce disruption of the sequence
**Definition:** Online shopping often breaks the natural visual-tactile-performance order.
**Class example:** On e-commerce sites, customers see the product (visual) but skip tactile and performance stages until after delivery, leading to returns if fit or look is unsatisfactory.
**Business example:** Myntra and Amazon Fashion face high return rates because customers can only judge tactile and performance quality after the product physically arrives.
**Exam tip:** This is a good point to raise in any question about challenges of digital retail versus physical retail.

## Case Discussion: Marketing Jewelry to Children

**Definition:** The class debated whether it is appropriate to position and advertise a jewelry product specifically for eight-year-old children.

**Points raised in favour:**
- In some cultures, such as Bengali culture, children commonly wear jewelry, so the positioning feels normal.
- Children are maturing faster today, making them a more viable consumer segment.

**Concerns raised:**
- Children are easily influenced by advertising and may pressure parents into buying.
- Advertising to children can increase peer pressure among young consumers.
- Traditional advertising logic advises against targeting children directly or using children as characters in ads, though it was noted that this "old world logic" may not fully apply to modern markets.

**Business example:** Indian jewelry brands like Tanishq have occasionally faced public debate over how they represent family and children in ad campaigns, similar to the ethical concerns raised in class.
**Exam tip:** If asked about ethics in advertising, use this case to discuss the tension between market opportunity and responsible advertising to vulnerable audiences.

## What the faculty stressed

- The brand name and logo are compulsory in every ad; nothing else is.
- Students must review the uploaded advertising slides and study the mentioned industry figures in advance for the midterm.
- Groups for the CIA assignment were deliberately assigned by the faculty rather than chosen by students, to break familiar friend-group dynamics.
- The Usha CIA assignment must strictly retain brand name, product category, and punchline, even though everything else can be reimagined.
- Only one submission per group is needed, but all member names and registration numbers must appear in the comments.
- The silent communication sequence (visual, tactile, performance) must occur in that exact order in traditional retail, and this order is disrupted in e-commerce.

- **CIA 1 (Usha Ad Reimagining):** Group assignment, static poster format only. Retain Usha brand name, sewing machine product, and "Can't buy better" punchline. Groups are faculty-assigned (listed above). Submit one poster per group with all member names and registration numbers in the comments.

## Practice questions

**Q1.** Differentiate between copy and body copy in advertising, with an example.
**A:** Copy refers to the entire ad layout, including all visual and textual elements shown to the client before media release. Body copy is only the written text within that layout. A minimalistic ad can have no body copy at all and still rely heavily on white space, but the full layout is still called copy.

**Q2.** Explain the three-step silent communication sequence between a product and a customer.

Prof Sachin Sinha used this class to look at how every element of the marketing mix communicates, using the VTP (Visual, Tactile, Performance) scheme, price equations, place cues and the promotion toolkit. The second part moved to advertising itself: its philosophy, its tricks (converting the mundane to the magical, puffery), product identification through packaging and labeling, regulation by ASCI, and the formal AMA definition. The afternoon session analysed advertising appeals through Snickers and a "missing person" garment ad, and worked through the Incredible India campaign as a full case of global tourism communication.

## Key terms

| Term | Meaning | Class example |
|---|---|---|
| VTP scheme | Visual, Tactile and Performance cues a product or service sends before and during purchase | Garments: look, feel of fabric, trial room fit |
| Promotion toolkit | Advertising, publicity, public relations, direct marketing, personal selling | Diagram of the 4 Ps in communication form |
| Price-Quality (PQ) equation | Belief that a higher price means higher quality | General consumer assumption |
| Price-Status (PS) equation | High-value purchases used to project social status | Conspicuous consumption by the Indian middle class |
| Conspicuous consumption | Buying expensive or luxury goods to show off status | Linked to India's colonial past and low self-esteem |
| Reasonable price range | Mental lower and upper price limit a buyer holds | Price below the lower limit makes buyers doubt quality |
| Puffery | Exaggeration in ads not meant as a factual claim, hard to challenge in court | Real estate ads near Buddh International Circuit |
| Grade labeling | Labels that certify grade or standard | UPC barcode, veg/non-veg dot, FSSAI, ISI, Hallmark |
| Descriptive labeling | Labels that describe the product's details | Expiry date, ingredients, manufacturer address |
| ASCI | Advertising Standards Council of India, a self-regulatory watchdog | Dabur Honey vs Patanjali dispute |
| Advertising (AMA) | Paid, non-personal presentation of goods, services and ideas by an identified sponsor | Paid space in newspapers, TV, radio, social media |
| Advertising appeal | The core idea or emotion an ad uses to move the audience | Snickers humour appeal |

## Communication through the marketing mix

### Every P communicates

**Definition:** Each of the four Ps (product, price, place, promotion) sends a message to the customer, so each has a "communication version". Promotion is only the most visible one.
**Class example:** The professor showed a diagram mapping the communication version of all four elements of the marketing mix.
**Business example:** Maruti Suzuki runs separate Arena and Nexa showrooms. The place itself tells you which cars are premium before any salesperson speaks.
**Exam tip:** When asked about IMC, show that communication is wider than advertising. Product design, price and outlet all carry messages.

### The traditional promotion toolkit

**Definition:** The five classic promotion tools are advertising, publicity, public relations, direct marketing and personal selling.
**Class example:** Listed while reviewing the 4 Ps diagram; sales promotion was discussed separately later in class.
**Business example:** A car launch by Tata Motors typically combines TV advertising, press coverage (publicity), a launch event (PR), SMS and email offers (direct marketing) and dealership sales staff (personal selling).
**Remember:** Five tools: A, P, PR, DM, PS.

### Brand recovery through communication

**Definition:** After a negative event, a brand uses well-produced communication to rebuild customer confidence.
**Class example:** After the Fly Dubai aircraft incident involving an Indian pilot, the airline released a series of high-quality advertisements to restore trust in its services.
**Business example:** After the 2003 worm controversy, Cadbury India ran "Project Vishwas" and brought in Amitabh Bachchan for reassurance ads, along with new sealed packaging. Nestle's Maggi ran a "We miss you too" style comeback campaign after its 2015 ban.

## The VTP communication scheme

### Visual (V)

**Definition:** Unspoken communication from the appearance and look of a good before purchase.
**Class example:** The first look of a garment on the rack. In services, students often choose a university based on the campus ambiance.
**Business example:** Tanishq showrooms use lighting, display and interiors to signal trust and premium quality the moment you walk in.

### Tactile (T)

**Definition:** Communication through touch and feel, often used to judge quality.
**Class example:** Feeling the fabric of a garment (a habit more common among older generations). In cars, the physical comfort of the seat and the leg space. In services, tactile communication is often inconsistent: what you feel during admission can differ from the experience after enrolment.
**Business example:** Raymond stores let you handle fabric bolts before ordering a suit, because feel is a key quality signal for suiting.

### Performance (P)

**Definition:** Communication based on how the product actually works or fits when used, the "try out" phase.
**Class example:** Trial rooms for clothes, test drives for cars, fittings for tailored bridal wear, a fruit vendor offering a grape or cutting a piece of fruit for you to taste. In services, coaching centres run demo classes so students can trial before paying.
**Business example:** Lenskart's home try-on and in-store trials let you check frames on your face before buying. Car brands such as Hyundai and Tata Motors offer home test drives.

### VTP across product categories

**Definition:** The relative weight of V, T and P changes by category.
**Class example:** Garments use all three. Automobiles rely heavily on tactile comfort and performance (test drive). For fruits and vegetables, visual appeal may matter less than touch and taste.
**Business example:** FMCG food brands use in-store sampling at retail chains like DMart and Reliance Smart because taste (performance) convinces more than the pack.
**Exam tip:** Apply VTP to both a good and a service in your answer. The class covered services (university, coaching) as well as goods.

## Price communication

### Price-Quality (PQ) equation

**Definition:** The general assumption that a higher price signals higher quality.
**Class example:** Discussed as the most common price equation in consumer minds.
**Business example:** Premium mattress and appliance brands often price above the market so buyers infer better quality.

### Price-Technology (PT) equation

**Definition:** The assumption that a higher price means more advanced technology.
**Class example:** Higher-priced products are associated with newer technology.
**Business example:** Dyson prices its vacuum cleaners and hair dryers far above Indian rivals, and buyers read the price as a signal of superior engineering.

### Price-Status (PS) equation

**Definition:** High-value purchases are used to project social status.
**Class example:** Linked directly to conspicuous consumption by the Indian middle class.
**Business example:** Many Indian buyers take an iPhone on EMI partly because the brand signals status.

### Conspicuous consumption

**Definition:** Buying luxury or expensive products mainly to display status in society. The term was coined by Thorstein Veblen in *The Theory of the Leisure Class* (1899) (textbook).
**Class example:** The professor linked this urge in the Indian middle class to the colonial past: being ruled by the British left a lingering low self-esteem that consumers try to compensate for through material display. The word "conspicuous" has biological roots, referring to the bright colours of flower petals that attract bees for pollination. The class debated whether Gen Z still behaves this way or whether it was stronger in earlier generations.
**Business example:** Luxury car brands like Mercedes-Benz and BMW, and big fat Indian weddings, are classic Indian cases of status display.
**Remember:** Conspicuous = designed to be noticed, like a petal attracting a bee.

### Reasonable price

**Definition:** Consumers carry a mental price range with a lower and an upper limit. A price above the upper limit is too costly; a price below the lower limit makes them doubt the quality and reject the product.
**Class example:** Discussed as the reason "too cheap" can fail.
**Business example:** The Tata Nano was marketed as the "cheapest car", and the tag put off buyers who did not want to be seen in a cheap car. Ratan Tata later admitted the "cheapest car" label was a mistake.
**Exam tip:** Link reasonable price to the PQ equation. Low price can send a negative quality message.

## Place communication

**Definition:** The point of purchase itself acts as a marketing and communication tool.
**Class example:** Branded carry bags, such as Big Bazaar bags, once served as fashion statements and objects of prestige for Indian consumers. The professor referred to writer Rama Pija worker [Rama Bijapurkar], who writes about the unique and often ironic nature of the Indian consumer.
**Business example:** Shoppers reuse premium store bags from brands like Zara or Apple, so the bag keeps advertising the store after the sale.
**Remember:** Rama Bijapurkar's well-known book on Indian consumers is *We Are Like That Only* (textbook).

## Sales promotion

**Definition:** Incentivising purchase through discounts and special schemes for a limited period.
**Class example:** In India, sales promotion is often culturally endorsed. Dhanteras encourages buying something new (traditionally steel utensils), so the festival acts as a cultural driver for sales.
**Business example:** Jewellers such as Tanishq run Dhanteras offers on making charges, and Flipkart's Big Billion Days and Amazon's Great Indian Festival are timed around Diwali.
**Exam tip:** Mention cultural endorsement as an India-specific feature of sales promotion.

## Publicity and public relations

**Definition:** Activities that build visibility and goodwill, ranging from high-end events to low-cost distribution of material.
**Class example:**
- High-end: the Auto Expo for vehicles, Apple's annual Keynote events for iPhone launches.
- Low-cost: leaflets, pamphlets and business cards handed out at malls.
- Innovative: for an Aamir Khan film (likely *Ghajini*, 2008), multiplex staff sported the film's haircut to create a cultural connection.
- Outdoor: billboards and political-style road shows.
**Business example:** Reliance announces major Jio launches at its Annual General Meeting, which generates huge free media coverage.

## Experiential marketing

**Definition:** Creating an immersive experience around the product so the customer feels it, not just sees it.
**Class example:** A horror film (named in class as Kaalo / Vastu Shastra) set up cinema lobbies with black magic themes, artificial fire and ushers dressed as ghosts. Reliance Jio's launch used a high-profile Mumbai event with Aamir Khan, Shah Rukh Khan and Sachin Tendulkar to build massive visibility.
**Business example:** Car brands set up off-road test tracks at the Auto Expo so visitors experience the vehicle's performance first hand.

## Product identification: branding, packaging and labeling

### Packaging

**Definition:** Packaging is of two main types. Protective packaging focuses on safety and preservation. Aesthetic packaging focuses on decoration, convenience and visual appeal.
**Class example:** Discussed as part of product identification alongside branding and labeling.
**Business example:** Amul's Tetra Pak milk is protective packaging that keeps milk safe for months. Cadbury Celebrations gift boxes are aesthetic packaging built for festive gifting.

### Grade labeling

**Definition:** Labels that certify grade, standard or category.
**Class example:** Barcodes (Universal Product Code, UPC), red and green dots for non-veg and veg, FSSAI licence, ISI mark, Hallmark for jewellery.
**Business example:** BIS hallmarking of gold jewellery became mandatory in India in 2021, so every Tanishq or Kalyan piece carries the hallmark.

### Descriptive labeling

**Definition:** Labels that describe the product's details.
**Class example:** Expiry date, manufacturing and packing dates, ingredients, manufacturer address, and regional sales restrictions (for example, books "for sale in India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka only").
**Business example:** A Maggi noodles pack lists ingredients, nutrition facts, MRP, best-before date and Nestle India's address.
**Exam tip:** Grade = certifies standard. Descriptive = tells you facts about the product. Give two examples of each.

## The philosophy of advertising

### What advertising is

**Definition:** The professor described advertising as the science of arresting human intelligence long enough to make money, often by turning mundane experiences into magical ones through illusion.
**Class example:** Advertising works like a magic show: it suspends the customer's natural intelligence and rational thinking.
**Business example:** Cadbury Dairy Milk's "Kuch Meetha Ho Jaye" turned eating a chocolate into a celebration ritual.

### Etymology

**Definition:** "Advertise" comes from the Latin word advertia [advertere], meaning to turn one's attention towards something.
**Class example:** Used to explain that the first job of an ad is to capture attention.
**Business example:** Amul's topical hoardings grab attention by commenting on current news.

### Positioning

**Definition:** Creating a specific value spot or space for the brand in the customer's mind. The idea was popularised by Al Ries and Jack Trout (textbook).
**Class example:** Discussed as the purpose behind advertising messages.
**Business example:** Fevicol owns "strong bond" in Indian minds through its humorous ads.

### Mesmerising the audience

**Definition:** Being so overwhelmed by oratory or performance that you lose your sense of right and wrong. The word comes from Lord Mesmer [Franz Anton Mesmer, an 18th-century German physician known for "animal magnetism"].
**Class example:** Ads aim to mesmerise viewers the way a magician does.
**Business example:** Celebrity-heavy launch films hold viewers through star power more than product facts.

## Converting the mundane to the magical

**Definition:** Advertising takes ordinary, repetitive tasks and shows them as joyful or magical experiences.
**Class example:**
- Detergent and dishwashing ads showing people cherishing stain removal.
- Christ University promotional films showing students and teachers far more active and enthusiastic than in daily classes.
- Pen ads showing students enjoying writing during an exam.
- Home appliance ads showing cooking and cleaning as an overflow of love rather than daily drudgery.
**Business example:** Surf Excel's "Daag Achhe Hain" turned dirty clothes into a sign of a child's good deeds.

## Puffery: the "legalized lie"

**Definition:** Exaggeration in advertising that is not meant to be taken as a factual claim, so it cannot easily be challenged in court.
**Class example:**
- Shampoo ads promising impossible shine, strength or length.
- Toothpaste ads with spotless white teeth and perfect gums.
- Real estate ads near the Buddh International Circuit (Formula 1 track) showing residents watching races from their balconies, which is physically impossible.
- Flipkart Big Billion Day ads using an excessive number of celebrities and long durations to build hype.
**Business example:** Red Bull's "Red Bull gives you wings" is a famous puffery line; Thums Up's "Taste the Thunder" works the same way.
**Remember:** Puffery is vague and subjective. A specific, measurable false claim is misleading advertising, not puffery.

## Regulation and ethics

**Definition:** The Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI) is a self-regulatory watchdog that checks whether ads follow ethical norms. It is a watchdog, not a law enforcement body.
**Class example:** Compared with sector regulators IRDA [IRDAI] (insurance), TRAI (telecom) and SEBI (securities). Cases mentioned: the legal dispute between Dabur Honey and Patanjali over claims of authenticity and purity, and Patanjali's claims of a corona cure.
**Business example:** Patanjali's Coronil was promoted as a COVID cure; the AYUSH Ministry asked it to stop such claims, and in 2024 the Supreme Court pulled up Patanjali over misleading ads. ASCI's 2021 influencer guidelines require disclosure tags such as #ad.
**Exam tip:** Distinguish ASCI (self-regulation, advisory) from statutory regulators (IRDAI, TRAI, SEBI) that have legal powers.

## Formal definition of advertising (AMA)

**Definition:** The American Marketing Association defines advertising as a paid form of non-personal presentation of goods, services and ideas by an identified sponsor.
**Class example:**
- Paid: advertising cannot be free, because you must buy space or airtime in a medium (newspaper, social media, TV, radio).
- Non-personal: it is mass communication aimed at the public, with no one-to-one interaction between sponsor and receiver.
**Business example:** HUL buys TV airtime during IPL matches for Surf Excel; HUL is the identified sponsor, the message is paid and goes to millions at once.
**Remember:** Four parts: paid, non-personal, goods/services/ideas, identified sponsor. Publicity fails the "paid" test; personal selling fails the "non-personal" test.

## Advertising appeals

### What an appeal is

**Definition:** An appeal is the central approach an ad uses to attract attention and move the audience, such as humour, fear, emotion or curiosity. Appeals are usually grouped as rational or emotional (textbook).
**Class example:** The professor said the mid-term and end-term exams will focus heavily on appeals, so you should be able to name the appeal in any ad and explain how it works.
**Business example:** Fevicol uses humour, Dettol uses fear of germs, and Cadbury's festive ads use warmth and family emotion.
**Exam tip:** Use drawings and doodles to explain an ad in your answer script. The professor encourages visuals over long text.

### Humour appeal: Snickers

**Definition:** A humour appeal uses comedy to make the message memorable and likeable.
**Class example:** Snickers ads show that hunger makes people act abnormally, for example claiming to love Mondays. Eating a Snickers restores their normal self.
**Business example:** Mars' global "You're not you when you're hungry" campaign was adapted in India with characters turning back into themselves after a bite.
**Remember:** Snickers formula: hunger = not yourself; Snickers = normal again.

### Curiosity and alarm: the "missing" garment ad

**Definition:** An ad that copies a familiar format, such as a public notice, to create alarm and curiosity so the reader stops and reads.
**Class example:** A garment store ad was designed like a public notice for a missing person, with a "missing" headline. Its content compared choosing a bride with choosing a wedding outfit.
**Business example:** Amul's topical hoardings borrow news headlines in a similar way to grab instant attention.

### Ethics of deceptive formats

**Definition:** Creative ads can cross into deception when they imitate official or serious formats or make offensive comparisons.
**Class example:** The class debated whether copying a missing person notice to sell clothes is unethical or simply creative. The bride vs outfit comparison was flagged as absurd and possibly offensive.
**Business example:** ASCI regularly upholds complaints against ads found to mislead or to demean women.
**Exam tip:** In appeal questions, add one line on ethics. It shows judgement, and the class discussed it directly.

## Case study: the Incredible India campaign

### Origins and objective

**Definition:** A national tourism campaign that brings a whole country under one brand to attract foreign visitors.
**Class example:**
- Launched in 2002 by the Ministry of Tourism, Government of India.
- The timing followed the 9/11 attacks of 2001, which had hit global travel and India's tourist arrivals.
- It united the state tourism boards under one banner to create a single image of India.
- "Atithi Devo Bhava" (the guest is God) was part of the same effort to welcome foreign guests.
**Business example:** Kerala Tourism's "God's Own Country" ran as a strong state brand, and Incredible India gave such state efforts one national umbrella.
**Remember:** 2002, Ministry of Tourism, post 9/11, one banner for all states.

### Market-specific execution

**Definition:** Adapting the creative message to each target city while keeping one campaign identity.
**Class example:**
- London: electronic posters on buses with yoga practitioners and the line "go back to 3000 BC and get a healthier life", positioning India as the home of ancient wellness.
- Paris: magazines in executive lounges at Charles de Gaulle Airport showing temples, mosques and churches with the line "God created man, and man is returning the favour by building houses for God."
- New York: LED displays in Times Square on Valentine's Day Eve (13 February) showing the Taj Mahal, a sarcastic dig at flowers and chocolates compared with the Taj as a gift of love.
**Business example:** McDonald's India builds local ads around the McAloo Tikki while keeping the global brand, the same "one brand, local message" logic.
**Exam tip:** Match each city to its appeal: London = health, Paris = spirituality and architecture, New York = love and romance.

### Media and partnerships

**Definition:** Choosing media that reach the exact target audience and adding partners who make travel easier.
**Class example:**
- Niche magazines such as Architectural Digest, Overdrive and Inside Outside to reach high-society readers.
- BBC, CNN and National Geographic for European markets.
- The website was translated into several European languages.
- Visa and American Express tie-ups offered cash-back and discounts to tourists.
**Business example:** Taj Hotels partners with credit card issuers and luxury travel magazines to reach affluent international travellers.

### Crisis management and cultural promotion

**Definition:** Using communication to restore confidence after a disaster and to sell the country's culture as an experience.
**Class example:** After the December 2004 tsunami hit coastal areas and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, the government worked to restore tourist confidence. In Berlin, the campaign staged mock marriages to tap global interest in the "Big Fat Indian Wedding".
**Business example:** Kerala Tourism ran campaigns to bring tourists back after the 2018 floods, presenting the state as safe and open again.
**Remember:** The campaign responded to two crises: 9/11 and the 2004 tsunami.

## What the faculty stressed

- Communication is wider than promotion. Product (VTP), price and place all send messages.
- Apply VTP to services as well as goods: campus ambiance, admission feel vs reality, demo classes.
- The three price equations (PQ, PT, PS) and the reasonable price range.
- Conspicuous consumption in the Indian middle class and its colonial roots.
- India-specific cultural drivers like Dhanteras for sales promotion.
- Advertising suspends rational thinking and converts the mundane to the magical.
- Puffery as the "legalized lie" and the role of ASCI.
- The AMA definition, especially "paid" and "non-personal".
- Appeals will carry heavy weight in the mid-term and end-term exams.
- Use drawings and doodles in answer scripts to explain concepts.
- The Incredible India case: timing, one national banner, city-specific creatives, niche media and partnerships.
- Read Rama Bijapurkar's work on Indian consumers.

## Assignments and deadlines

- Google the work of Rama Pija worker [Rama Bijapurkar] to understand the unique traits of Indian consumers.
- Go through the additional theory slides shared by the professor before the mid-term exam. Some exam questions may come from slide material not discussed in class.

## Practice questions

**Q1.** Explain the VTP communication scheme with one example each from a product and a service.
**A:** VTP stands for Visual, Tactile and Performance cues. For a garment, visual is its look on the rack, tactile is the feel of the fabric, and performance is the fit in the trial room. For a coaching centre, visual is the classroom ambiance, tactile is the feel of the admission process, and performance is a free demo class before you pay.

**Q2.** What are the PQ, PT and PS equations in price communication?
**A:** The Price-Quality equation is the belief that a higher price means higher quality. The Price-Technology equation links higher price with more advanced technology, as with Dyson appliances. The Price-Status equation is the use of expensive purchases to project social status, which drives conspicuous consumption.

**Q3.** What is puffery? Why is it called a "legalized lie"?
**A:** Puffery is exaggeration in ads that is not meant to be taken as a factual claim, such as shampoo promising impossible shine or real estate ads showing F1 races from balconies near the Buddh International Circuit. Since no reasonable person treats it as fact, it is hard to challenge in court. ASCI steps in when exaggeration becomes a misleading factual claim, as with Patanjali's corona cure claims.

**Q4.** Analyse the Snickers advertising campaign in terms of its appeal.
**A:** Snickers uses a humour appeal. Its ads show that hunger makes people act unlike themselves, such as claiming to love Mondays, and a bite of Snickers brings them back to normal. The humour makes the ad memorable and ties the product to one clear benefit: it fixes hunger.

**Q5.** Define advertising as per the AMA and explain its key components.
**A:** The AMA defines advertising as a paid form of non-personal presentation of goods, services and ideas by an identified sponsor. It is paid because the sponsor must buy space or airtime in a medium. It is non-personal because it is mass communication with no one-to-one interaction, and the sponsor is identified, which separates it from publicity.

**Q6.** How did the Incredible India campaign adapt its message to different global markets?
**A:** Launched in 2002 after 9/11 hit travel, the campaign put all states under one banner but changed its creative by city. London buses showed yoga with "go back to 3000 BC and get a healthier life", Paris airport lounges carried temples, mosques and churches, and Times Square showed the Taj Mahal on Valentine's Day Eve. Niche magazines, BBC, CNN, National Geographic and Visa and American Express tie-ups supported the message.

This first RTM class, taught by Prof Manish Kumar Srivastava, framed retail as a practice you live rather than a process you memorise. It used the Indian mobile phone market to show how liberalisation, pricing psychology and consumer finance shaped retail, and closed with homework on market tracking and leasing.

## Key terms

| Term | Meaning | Class example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Psychological pricing | Setting prices just below a round number so they feel cheaper | ₹1,999 instead of ₹2,000 |
| Liberalisation | Opening an economy to private and foreign firms | India's 1991 reforms under Finance Minister Dr Manmohan Singh |
| Consumer finance | Credit that lets buyers pay in instalments | EMI on a scooter |
| Mono-brand store | A store that sells only one brand | Covered in detail on 15 Sep |
| Commercial leasing | Renting retail or office space for business use | Homework topic |
| Silent learning | Picking up vocabulary by reading slides on your own | Reading ahead without being told |

## How this course runs

- The next two years are "a bus journey to a destination". Observe the market and bring questions to class.
- CIA work is group-based, not individual.
- Keep a list of questions you cannot answer yet and bring them back.
- Take skill courses tied to your sector, such as AI in retail, and visit IIM campuses to see how others learn.
- Expect reflection writing at the end of many classes.

**Exam tip:** Retail answers score better with a live market example. Keep a running list of retail news: store openings, closures, pricing moves.

## Pricing psychology

**Definition:** Psychological pricing sets a price just under a round figure, because buyers read the left-most digit first and feel the product is cheaper.
**Class example:** ₹1,999 feels much cheaper than ₹2,000, though the gap is ₹1.
**Business example:** Bata has priced shoes at figures like ₹499 and ₹999 for decades. The ".99" ending became part of how Indian shoppers read Bata prices as good value.
**Remember:** Marketing works on human psychology to drive spending. Pricing is often the first place that psychology shows up.

## Case: the Indian mobile phone market

### Liberalisation opened the door

**Definition:** Liberalisation means removing controls so private and foreign firms can enter a market.
**Class example:** After the 1991 reforms under Dr Manmohan Singh as Finance Minister, global brands such as Nokia entered India. The class placed Nokia's rise around 1997 to 1998.
**Business example:** India's first mobile phone call was made on 31 July 1995, on a Nokia handset, between West Bengal Chief Minister Jyoti Basu and Telecom Minister Sukh Ram. Nokia went on to lead the Indian handset market for over a decade.

### Crowded wholesale and the value segment

**Class example:** Delhi's Sadar Bazar shows how crowded and price-driven wholesale markets are.
**Class example:** Micromax entered with cheap phones and grew into rural India. The phone repair market alone is worth crores.
**Business example:** Micromax briefly became one of India's top smartphone sellers around 2014, then lost share quickly once Chinese brands such as Xiaomi offered better specifications at similar prices. Value alone did not protect it.
**Exam tip:** Use Nokia and Micromax together to show two retail lessons: entry after liberalisation, and why a pure price position is fragile.

## Why Indian consumption is growing: four drivers

1. **Innovation** in products and services.
2. **Social media marketing** that reaches wider audiences.
3. **Rising investment** in the sector.
4. **Easy consumer finance**, through EMIs, UPI and Google Pay.

**Definition:** Consumer finance is credit that lets buyers spread payment over time.
**Class example:** EMIs make a scooter affordable. A hospital lets a patient finance the unpaid ₹5,000 of a ₹10,000 bill so they can leave hours earlier.
**Business example:** UPI, launched by NPCI in 2016, made instant payments normal even at small kiranas. Bajaj Finance built a large business on EMI cards used at electronics and appliance stores, turning big purchases into small monthly payments.
**Remember:** Payment ease is a retail growth driver in its own right. Fewer steps to pay means more completed sales.

## Store types introduced

**Definition:** A mono-brand store sells only one brand. Full coverage came on 15 Sep.
**Business example:** India has allowed up to 100% foreign investment in single-brand retail through the automatic route since 2018. IKEA opened its first Indian store in Hyderabad the same year.

## Learning habits the faculty asked for

**Definition:** Silent learning means reading a slide on your own and absorbing its vocabulary without being told.
**Key idea:** Retail is learned by observing. Watch what shops do, then ask why.

## What the faculty stressed

- Observe the market every day and bring your questions to class.
- Marketing and pricing work on human psychology.
- Consumer finance and payment ease are major growth drivers in India.
- CIA work will be in groups.

## Assignments and deadlines

- Download the assigned PDF report and use AI to turn it into a PPT.
- Find material on commercial or corporate leasing.
- Register on the two business and marketing websites he recommended.
- Track current market events (what happened and why) for the reflection class on 9 Sep at 8:30 am.

## Practice questions

**Q1.** What is psychological pricing? Give a class example and a real brand example.
**A:** It is pricing just below a round number so the product feels cheaper, because buyers read the first digit. In class, ₹1,999 felt far cheaper than ₹2,000. Bata's long use of prices like ₹499 and ₹999 is a real example.

**Q2.** Explain how the 1991 reforms changed Indian retail, using the mobile phone market.
**A:** Liberalisation allowed global brands to enter India. Nokia came in and dominated handsets for over a decade. The open market also let low-cost players like Micromax grow into rural India, which widened retail reach.

**Q3.** List the four drivers of Indian consumption growth discussed in class.
**A:** Innovation in products and services, social media marketing, rising investment, and easy consumer finance. The last includes EMIs and instant payments such as UPI and Google Pay.

**Q4.** Why is a pure low-price position risky for a retailer or brand? Use Micromax.
**A:** A low price is easy to copy. Micromax grew on cheap phones but lost share quickly when Xiaomi and others offered better specifications at similar prices. Without another advantage, price alone could not hold customers.

**Q5.** How does consumer finance increase retail sales? Give two examples.
**A:** It lets buyers spread cost over time, so bigger purchases become affordable now. Bajaj Finance EMI cards turn appliances into monthly payments, and a hospital financing part of a bill lets a patient pay later.
